title: bug(examples/linearlite): whole-board :populates makes independent successful writes last-reply-wins
description:
SURFACE REVIEW: examples/capabilities/resources/linearlite at afe446ea71bf7d0eb2e4ce5960caca864a091778.

SUMMARY

Linearlite is the flagship optimistic-mutation example and explicitly promises that accepted writes settle from recorded facts, "not whichever reply landed last" (examples/capabilities/resources/linearlite/README.md:58-65). Its implementation teaches the opposite cache consequence: every create, title edit, and status change replaces the single board resource with a whole-board snapshot from that mutation's response. Because those writes use independent mutation instances, each response can be accepted and the last response to arrive replaces the aggregate cache, even when its snapshot predates another accepted write.

This is not the ordinary same-instance stale-reply case. Mutation generation/work-id suppression is intentionally scoped to the reply's instance. It protects a re-execute of one instance; it cannot order independent instances that all write the same resource key. `:on-conflict :invalidate` also does not help: that policy governs a failed rollback, whereas an accepted success applies `:populates` authoritatively.

EVIDENCE

- README.md:58-65 says success re-seeds the board and that "No wall-clock race decides which wins" / the result is not "whichever reply landed last". README.md:76-80 says an instance's `:optimistic?` means its optimistic value is still on screen.
- core.cljs:147-158 defines one shared board target/query. Each mutation returns `{board-key result}` from `:populates`: create at :208-231, edit-title at :237-246, and change-status at :252-261.
- core.cljs:426-451 deliberately gives those writes distinct instances: `[:create tmp-id]`, `[:edit id]`, and `[:status id]`. Different cards and even title/status writes on one card can therefore be live independently.
- core.cljs:481-541 leaves create, edit, and status controls enabled while writes are pending, so overlap is an ordinary interaction, not an unsupported programmatic edge.
- The demo server freezes a whole-board value per request: `apply-write!` mutates and returns the then-current board at core.cljs:310-341; the HTTP stub captures that payload and defers its delivery by 220 ms at :343-387. Two quick writes therefore hold two different aggregate snapshots.
- The runtime verifier looks up only the mutation instance named by the reply (implementation/resources/src/re_frame/resources/mutation_events.cljc:1536-1571). On each accepted success it runs `apply-populates` unconditionally (:1640-1702). `apply-populates` seeds the target with the supplied value (:208-249), and `populate-entry` replaces `:data` (:291-327 in mutation_runtime.cljc). There is no cross-instance resource-target freshness verdict; that is outside the documented instance stale-suppression contract.
- Linearlite's behavioral tests cover one mutation at a time (implementation/adapters/reagent/test/re_frame/linearlite_example_cljs_test.cljs:354-465) and the real-stub tests inspect one write at a time (:569-635). The generic test named `concurrent-submissions-do-not-clobber` (resources_mutation_cljs_test.cljc:414-439) uses mutations with no cache consequences and asserts only that the two instance rows retain independent pending/result state; it cannot catch aggregate cache clobbering.
- Git history shows the whole-board `:populates` pattern originated with the example in c0e4889344; later edits changed prose, APIs, mounting, and the canned-503 classification, but did not add an overlapping-success witness or alter this consequence shape.

CONCRETE FAILURE

Start from board S. Dispatch A, which optimistically produces S+A and whose stub response freezes S+A. Before its delayed reply, dispatch independent B, which optimistically produces S+A+B and freezes S+A+B. When A settles first, its accepted whole-board populate replaces the cache with S+A: B vanishes from the screen even though B's instance remains pending and `:optimistic?` still derives true. B's later reply restores it, producing a visible optimistic regression in the shipped demo.

A real transport makes the issue worse. If two writes are processed in one order but their already-built responses arrive in the other, both independent instances are current and both whole-board populates are accepted. The older aggregate snapshot can arrive last and permanently erase an already-successful change in the client cache. Final cache state is then exactly last-reply-wins, contrary to the example's central claim.

IMPACT

This is teaching-surface correctness, not polish. The example invites SPA programmers and coding agents to copy independent per-control instances plus aggregate `:populates`, a combination that can lose accepted edits. It also makes the `:optimistic?` badge semantically dishonest during the overlap window. Because the README presents this as the safe answer to hand-written optimistic races, the example needs an honest concurrency shape before it is used as canonical guidance.

BOUNDED FIX

Keep the example small and choose one explicit, honest policy. Recommended: retain concurrent controls, but make success consequences commute at the same granularity as the writes. Have POST return the created issue plus enough correlation to replace its own temporary card, have title/status writes return the changed issue or field, and use surgical `:patches` over the board instead of replacing the whole aggregate from each independent response. Same-card/same-field re-executes should continue to reuse an instance so the existing stale-suppression rule applies. If the intended API only returns coarse board snapshots, an explicit invalidate/refetch or deliberate single-writer serialization is acceptable instead, but the example must not present independent whole-board response snapshots as order-independent.

Update the local README/comments to state the guarantee actually implemented. In particular, distinguish "the commit/rollback verdict uses recorded facts" from "independent successful server snapshots are globally ordered"; the latter is not supplied by mutation instance generations.

ACCEPTANCE

1. Add a focused Linearlite regression that dispatches two writes under distinct instances against the board, parks both transport replies, and settles them in both normal and reverse order.
2. After both accepted successes, the board contains both server-accepted changes; neither completion can revert the other's accepted field/card.
3. While the second write remains pending, settling the first does not erase the second optimistic change (or, if serialization is the chosen explicit policy, the UI cannot originate that overlap and the test pins the lock).
4. Preserve the example's headline behavior: each allowed write paints immediately, an unconflicted failure rolls back, a successful create reconciles its temporary id/marker, and existing single-write tests remain green.
5. README and source comments describe the bounded guarantee without claiming cross-instance whole-response ordering the runtime does not provide.
6. Exercise the actual example registrations/consequence functions, not test-local copies; the regression must fail against the current three whole-board `:populates` registrations.

NON-GOALS

- No generic cross-instance transaction scheduler, CRDT, vector-clock, or server version protocol in the resource runtime.
- No redesign of all resource granularity or every example.
- No change to the existing failed-rollback `:on-conflict` semantics.
- No broad UI polish, disabling campaign, or attempt to litigate every distributed-systems edge.

DUPLICATE AUDIT

Targeted `rg` searches of `.beads/issues.jsonl` for Linearlite plus whole-board/populate/out-of-order/last-reply/cache-clobber found no matching issue. Nearby beads are distinct: rf2-pqt5f fixed canned-503 classification; rf2-k4oe and rf2-djqm concern example-test registration ordering; rf2-ujdn0 concerns launch instructions; rf2-iy3d6 concerns RealWorld route/detail reply placement, not cross-instance mutation consequences.

UNCERTAINTY / VALIDATION NOTE

No runtime or browser command was run during this review, per the review fence. The static acceptance path is enough to prove that two distinct current instances can both replace the same resource entry; exact timer ordering in the canned browser should be pinned by the parked-reply regression rather than assumed. The recommended `:patches` shape is intentionally a bounded teaching fix; if maintainers prefer invalidate/refetch or explicit serialization, acceptance is behavioral rather than prescriptive.
close_reason:
REPRODUCED AND FIXED in the example. PR https://github.com/day8/re-frame2/pull/9197.

PREMISE HOLDS, and both halves of it. Two temporary tests planted in implementation/adapters/reagent/test/re_frame/linearlite_example_cljs_test.cljs (driving the example's own registrations, not copies) were RED on the unmodified example and GREEN after the fix, with identical inputs — captured exit 1 then 0, 13 tests / 61 assertions, the 11 pre-existing tests green in both runs. (a) Settling an accepted write erased another instance's STILL-PENDING optimistic change: srv-2 read :in-progress where :done was expected. (b) The older whole-board snapshot arriving LAST permanently reverted an already-ACCEPTED change: same read, both successes accepted. So the transient optimistic regression and the permanent last-reply-wins are both real, not one or the other.

OWNER: THE EXAMPLE, not the framework. implementation/ is untouched. :populates is documented as an authoritative load that seeds an entry from the reply and populate-entry does exactly that; :patches — (fn [params result] -> {target patch-fn}) — is the framework's existing tool for a fine-grained consequence, and the example's own README already called :optimistic 'the exact-target twin of a mutation's success-time :patches'. The bug was the example choosing the aggregate consequence for fine-grained independent writes.

FIX (examples/capabilities/resources/linearlite/** only, 2 files). Each mutation commits at the granularity it wrote at, so the three consequences are disjoint and commute: edit-title sets the saved title on its own card, change-status the saved status on its own card, create-issue drops its temporary card and merges in the server's row. The demo backend answers a write with just the row it changed, in the board's own {:issues [...]} envelope; a read still answers with the whole board. patch-issue is variadic so one shape serves both hooks. README and source comments now state the BOUNDED guarantee — the commit-or-roll-back verdict and same-instance stale-reply suppression are per-instance, independent instances writing one entry are not ordered for you and cannot be from the client, and keeping their consequences disjoint is the application's job — plus the honest alternatives (invalidate/refetch, or deliberate serialisation) when an API only returns coarse snapshots.

ACCEPTANCE 2-5 MET. Acceptance 1 and 6 met AS A REPRODUCTION but not as a landed test: examples are test-free by ruling (rf2-8cevm) so the witness cannot live under examples/, and its real home — the adapter test tree — was outside this worker's fence. The tests were run there and removed; that file is byte-identical to its committed blob f7c581dd8e8ec8d703b4456b6e58e5f13af1285a, verified by content hash. rf2-chl2 carries the verbatim test source so the durable regression is a paste-and-run job, and notes the two stale :populates references left behind (the passing-but-misnamed successful-write-commits-the-server-board-via-populates, and the frozen, uncompiled pilot baseline under docs/design/hicasso/product/pilots/baseline/linearlite/).

GATES on the final rebased base, captured exits: npm run test:cljs 0 (11176 tests / 55753 assertions / 0 failures); npm run test:examples-compile 0 (58 builds, zero warnings, [:examples/linearlite] among them); scripts/check_readme_links.py --ci 0, and that gate was checked for discrimination rather than trusted — a planted broken anchor in this README returned exit 1 naming file and line.

title: reagent-slim: ordinary after-render callbacks can precede the React 19 DOM commit
description:
## Correctness finding

`reagent2.core/after-render` promises to run after the next React commit, but reagent-slim's ordinary production microtask path can invoke the callback while React 19 still exposes the old DOM. This is a live-path ordering bug, not a request for broader Reagent compatibility.

## Exact evidence

- `implementation/adapters/reagent-slim/src/reagent2/impl/batching.cljs`: `RenderQueue.flush-queues` calls `ratom/flush!`, then `flush-render`, then `flush-after-render`. `flush-render` only invokes each dirty class's bare `.forceUpdate`; there is no React commit boundary or commit callback. Therefore "forceUpdate was requested" is treated as "React committed" before callbacks run.
- `implementation/adapters/reagent-slim/src/reagent2/dom/client.cljs`: the `flush-render!` implementation and its load-bearing comment document the opposite React-19 fact: under `createRoot`, bare `forceUpdate` outside a React batching boundary is scheduled rather than committed, and the DOM remains OLD when `batching/flush!` returns. That is why `flush-render!` wraps the same drain in `react-dom/flushSync`. Commit `3d89c29c61` records the browser proof: the post-flush assertion read the old value without that boundary.
- `implementation/adapters/reagent-slim/src/reagent2/core.cljs`: public `after-render` says "after the next React commit" and routes to `batching/do-after-render`. `implementation/adapters/reagent-slim/src/re_frame/adapter/reagent_slim.cljs` publishes that function as `:adapter/after-render`, so `re-frame.interop/after-render` reaches this exact queue.
- `implementation/adapters/reagent-slim/IMPL-SPEC.md` §2.3/§2.9/§4 repeats the post-render contract, while `spec/002-Frames.md` names after-render effects as the canonical "show this, then run the heavy block" replacement for queue-pausing. `tools/re-frame2-pair-mcp/src/re_frame2_pair_mcp/tools/dispatch.cljs` also treats the adapter hook as post-commit/pre-paint for `:await-render`.
- Existing slim coverage does not exercise this boundary. `implementation/adapters/reagent-slim/test/reagent2/impl/batching_cljs_test.cljs` uses fake JS objects whose `forceUpdate` body runs synchronously, so its `[:render :after]` assertion proves call order only. `implementation/adapters/reagent-slim/test/reagent2/dom/client_cljs_test.cljs` similarly uses fake components and/or `act`; `reagent_slim_flush_render_dom_cljs_test.cljs` tests the explicit `flushSync` API. `reagent_slim_late_bind_publication_cljs_test.cljs` pins hook publication, not DOM timing. There is no reagent-slim counterpart to the real-DOM post-commit assertion used by the React spine.
- Independent substrate comparison: the repository-pinned Reagent 2.0.1 `reagent.impl.batching/run-queue` wraps dirty component updates in an injected `react-flush`, and `reagent.dom.client/render` installs `react-dom/flushSync`; only after that wrapper returns does stock `flush-after-render` run. Slim copied the queue order but omitted the commit-bearing seam on its ordinary path.

## Concrete failure sequence and impact

A ratom/app-db change queues a slim component, and application or framework code queues an after-render callback. The shared microtask drains dependencies, calls bare `forceUpdate` (React schedules the class update), and immediately invokes the callback. The callback can read stale DOM. Worse, the documented long-running-work pattern can start its heavy block before React paints the requested "working" state, delaying the very feedback the API exists to provide. The Pair `:await-render` path is consequently founded on accidental later-rAF timing rather than the adapter hook's promised post-commit invariant.

## Recommended bounded fix

Make the ordinary scheduled queue defer `flush-after-render` until the dirty updates in that turn have actually committed. Keep `reagent2.impl.batching` host-neutral; a small client-installed commit wrapper (analogous to stock Reagent's `react-flush`) used when a pending after-render queue requires the guarantee is one plausible minimal shape. A reliable class-update commit callback is another. Let the real-DOM regression choose the smallest correct seam.

Preserve the current callback FIFO order, once-only drain, per-callback throw isolation, no-dirty callback behavior, next-turn cascade rule, and explicit `flush-render!`/`flush-views!` semantics. Reconcile the local docstrings/IMPL-SPEC only where they currently equate a bare `forceUpdate` call with a completed render.

## Posture and non-goals

This repair makes a retained minimal API tell the truth and directly supports responsive SPA feedback. Do not add a general scheduler abstraction, copy the React-spine driver-root machinery, expand the public API, emulate transitions/Suspense policy, or litigate arbitrary unmounted/cross-root edge cases. Do not globally force every ratom microtask synchronous merely as an easy workaround if a narrower commit-bearing path for queued after-render work preserves the intended React-19 concurrency.

## Duplicate and history search

Searched every current bead in every state across title, description, acceptance, design, and notes for `after-render`, `after render`, `flush-after-render`, `post-commit`, `commit phase`, `forceUpdate`, `stale DOM`, `React commit`, `microtask`, and reagent-slim/render variants. The only `after-render` matches were closed `rf2-6r9j.33` (stale IMPL-SPEC architecture prose) and closed `rf2-6r9j.44` (an unrelated SSR response parameter); neither owns runtime commit timing. Broader matches were unrelated surfaces. Git history searches for `flush-after-render`, `after-render`, `forceUpdate`, and `flushSync` found: initial scheduler commit `1d621015bd`, callback-throw isolation `a834ab9bbd`, and explicit synchronous `flush-render!` repair `3d89c29c61`; none repairs or tests the ordinary microtask path. The UIx post-commit work (`e616aabbbd` and shared-suite tests) is a different substrate implementation.

## Uncertainty

No new browser bundle was built in this review-only worker because the assigned worktree intentionally has no `node_modules` link and no source/test edits were authorized. The stale-DOM timing is nevertheless independently established by the current control flow, the stock-Reagent implementation, and this repository's prior React-19 browser failure/fix in `3d89c29c61`. The exact narrowest repair seam remains intentionally open; the required real-DOM ordinary-path test below resolves it behaviorally.
design: Favor the smallest commit-aware seam that keeps the queue node-safe and preserves ordinary concurrent behavior when no post-commit callback is pending. A client-installed wrapper around the dirty-component phase is worth testing because stock Reagent already demonstrates that shape; if used, avoid unnecessary `flushSync` on queue turns without after-render work and avoid double-drain/nested-boundary surprises under the existing explicit `flush-render!`. Acceptance is behavioral rather than prescribing that mechanism.
acceptance_criteria:
- Add `implementation/adapters/reagent-slim/test/re_frame/adapter/reagent_slim_after_render_dom_cljs_test.cljs` (or an equivalently named reagent-slim browser test) that installs the slim adapter, mounts a ratom/subscription-backed view through `reagent2.dom.client/create-root` + `render`, commits the initial value, changes the value, and calls `re-frame.interop/after-render`.
- In the callback, read the mounted node's `textContent` and prove it contains the new value; also assert the callback fires exactly once. The test must assert the old DOM before the scheduler turn so a synchronous mutation cannot make it vacuous.
- The regression must exercise the ordinary queued microtask path. It must not use `reagent2.dom.client/flush-views!`, adapter `flush-render!`, `react/act`, a manual `react-dom/flushSync` around the update/drain, or an extra `requestAnimationFrame` before the callback assertion, because each masks the defect.
- On the pre-fix implementation the test fails specifically because the callback observes the old committed DOM while the class update is only scheduled. On the fix it observes the new DOM after the actual commit under the repository's React 19 floor.
- `implementation/adapters/reagent-slim/src/reagent2/impl/batching.cljs` preserves callback FIFO/once-only/throw isolation, callbacks scheduled with no dirty component still fire asynchronously, and components queued during a drain remain for the next turn.
- `reagent_slim_flush_render_dom_cljs_test.cljs`, the focused batching tests, the slim node tests, and browser tests remain green. Any changed contract prose in `reagent2.core`, `batching.cljs`, or `IMPL-SPEC.md` agrees that after-render means post-commit, not merely after calling `forceUpdate`.
- The implementation stays private and bounded: no new public symbol and no broad React-spine/scheduler redesign.
notes: Review scope was `implementation/adapters/reagent-slim/**`; consumers/spec/history were read only to establish contract and impact. No tracked file was edited, no test artifact was created, and no bead was updated. Evidence is source/history-based with the remaining uncertainty explicitly captured in the description.
close_reason: CONFIRMED and FIXED. The premise held and was measured, not reasoned: on a real React 19 createRoot root, ordinary microtask path with no test primitive driving it, an after-render callback registered after a dispatch taking n=1 to n=2 was handed n=1. RenderQueue.flush-queues called ratom/flush!, then each dirty component's bare .forceUpdate, then the callbacks, with no commit boundary; under React 19 an update issued outside React's batching context is scheduled, not committed. Fix: the dirty-component pass now runs inside a host commit boundary that reagent2.dom.client INJECTS into reagent2.impl.batching/render-commit at ns-load (react-dom/flushSync), the same direction reagent2.ratom/rea-schedule is filled, so batching keeps requiring nothing of react-dom and a Node/SSR consumer without the DOM client keeps the bare drain. Gated on there actually being a callback waiting, so an ordinary reactive re-render is not promoted to discrete priority. Witness: reagent_slim_after_render_dom_cljs_test.cljs reads textContent from INSIDE the callback and asserts the OLD DOM between dispatch and callback so a synchronous commit could not satisfy it vacuously; no flush-views!, flush-render!, act, manual flushSync around the update/drain, or rAF before the read. Fails before (browser lane exit 1, one failure, actual (not (= "n=2" "n=1"))) and passes after (792 tests / 4280 assertions, 0 failures, same totals). FIFO, once-only, throw isolation, fire-with-nothing-dirty and next-turn cascade preserved and pinned. No new public symbol. spec/002-Frames.md and the pair-MCP dispatch.cljs were NOT changed: both already describe the hook as post-commit, which the repair makes true rather than prose needing revision. :advanced release (bundle-isolation) 0 warnings. PR #9209.

title: resources: owner-free conflict rollback drops stale key from :affected-keys
description:
## Scope

Repair optimistic-mutation conflict rollback in `implementation/resources/src/re_frame/resources/mutation_events.cljc` for an exact `:optimistic` target whose resource legitimately omits optional `:tags`. Add focused JVM/CLJS coverage through the public resource/mutation event path. Align the conflict-rule prose only where needed to state the corrected exact-key behavior.

## Correctness finding

The default `:on-conflict :invalidate` policy can silently keep a failed optimistic value as fresh cache truth. The rollback record already carries the exact canonical `:resource/key`, but `invalidate-conflicted-key-fx` throws that identity away and attempts to rediscover the entry through its current tags. It returns nil when `(seq (:tags entry))` is false. `settle-optimistic-rollback` then leaves every `:invalidate` disposition's current entry unchanged, emits no recovery effect for the tagless key, and nevertheless includes that key in `:refetched-keys`.

`:tags` is an optional resource key, and exact-target `:optimistic` does not require tags. Optional invalidation metadata therefore becomes an undocumented correctness prerequisite for automatic rollback recovery.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Register a resource with required `:scope` and `:params-schema`, but no optional `:tags`.
2. Ensure it under owner A and settle server value `{:saved? false}`.
3. Execute an exact-target optimistic mutation that changes the entry to `{:saved? true}`.
4. Before the mutation reply, ensure the still-fresh entry under owner B; `state/attach-owner` advances the revision, creating the contested rollback case.
5. Deliver the accepted mutation failure and inspect the entry plus captured managed-HTTP requests.

Observed: the entry remains `{:data {:saved? true}, :invalidated-at nil, :active-owners #{:owner/a :owner/b}, :revision 3}` and no recovery request is emitted. Adding only a `:tags` function makes the same sequence end `:fetching` with a current work id and a new recovery request.

## Concrete Evidence

- `spec/016-Resources.md:749` explicitly lists `:tags` among optional v1 registration keys.
- `spec/016-Resources.md:1045-1052` and `docs/resources/coming-from-tanstack-query.md:137` promise that a moved-revision rollback under the default policy marks the entry stale and lets the read path refetch authoritative truth.
- `implementation/resources/src/re_frame/resources/mutation_events.cljc:567-584` builds recovery only as `:rf.resource/invalidate-tags` and returns nil for an existing entry with no tags.
- `implementation/resources/src/re_frame/resources/mutation_events.cljc:609-635` restores only `:restore` dispositions; an `:invalidate` disposition is left untouched and its nil effect is dropped. Lines 639-642 then classify every such disposition as refetched whether an effect exists or not.
- The read-only public-path JVM reproduction above isolates the gate: tagless leaves fresh B/no request; the otherwise identical tagged control starts a recovery fetch.
- The resources JVM suite is green at 818 tests / 7,284 assertions. Its shared optimistic-settle fixture always supplies tags (`implementation/resources/test/re_frame/resources_optimistic_settle_cljs_test.cljc:91-96`), including the owner attach/release conflict cases at lines 417-489, so the allowed tagless branch is untested.

## Failure scenario / invariant

A settings/profile resource validly omits tags because callers address its one cache entry exactly. A save mutation applies an exact optimistic patch. While it is pending, another component attaches to the entry (or another authoritative entry write moves its revision). The save receives a 5xx. The conflict detector correctly refuses the stale snapshot, but tag-based recovery matches nothing; every subscribed view can show the server-rejected write indefinitely.

Invariant: for every surviving exact key with a default conflict disposition, rollback must preserve the concurrent entry/liveness state while making that exact entry stale and recoverable. Whether the resource declared unrelated tag-index metadata must not affect that outcome.

## Recommended minimal fix

Recover by the exact `:resource/key` already present in each rollback disposition. In the failure settle, mark the current surviving entry stale directly with the reply's causal completion time, preserve its current owners/work facts, and enqueue the ordinary exact resource refetch when it has active owners; an owner-free entry stays durably stale for its next ensure. Reuse or extract the existing single-entry invalidation/refetch mechanics rather than adding a second public invalidation API. Derive `:reconciliation-refetches` and trace `:refetched` from requests actually enqueued, not merely from the disposition name.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A handler-level CLJC test uses only public registration/dispatch surfaces to register an exact-target resource with no `:tags`, load server value A, execute an optimistic mutation to B, move the revision via a second owner attach, then settle with an accepted error. Both owners survive, the exact entry is made stale, an active-owner recovery request is issued, and settling it with A makes the public resource subscription return A rather than failed B.
- The same test is paired with the tagged control and proves removing only `:tags` no longer changes recovery. Before the fix, the tagless arm must fail on fresh B/no request while the tagged control passes.
- An owner-free conflict arm proves the exact entry becomes durably stale without creating liveness or fetching immediately; a later public ensure starts recovery. This distinguishes stale from refetched and prevents an always-fetch fix.
- The existing no-conflict failure arm still restores `:before` verbatim and issues no recovery request; `:on-conflict :force` remains unchanged.
- Rollback trace and `:patch-summary :reconciliation-refetches` name only requests actually scheduled. A tagless conflicted entry is never reported refetched while remaining fresh with zero requests.
- A focused negative control that reinstates the `seq :tags` gate or disables exact-key staling makes the new tagless assertion fail. All resources JVM and CLJS suites pass normally.

## Non-goals

- Do not make `:tags` required or synthesize hidden tags.
- Do not broaden invalidation across scopes, scan the cache, or change `:optimistic-tags` targeting.
- Do not change `:on-conflict :force`, no-conflict restoration, resource identity, or public event grammar.
- No generic invalidation framework, compatibility layer, or unrelated runtime refactor.

## Related/duplicate search

Full all-status title searches for `optimistic`, `rollback`, `conflict`, `tagless`, and `untagged`, plus all-status description searches for `on-conflict`, `optimistic-rolled-back`, `reconciliation-refetches`, `entry's own tags`, `no tags`, `failed optimistic`, and `stale optimistic`, found no matching issue. `rf2-e4y9` (closed) concerns malformed optimistic targets deleting a write before transport; distinct. `rf2-9n43e` (open) concerns the RealWorld demo backend discarding server-side write state; distinct. The sole in-progress bead, `rf2-jui1c`, is an unrelated prose sweep.
notes:
TRIAGE 2026-08-31 19:38:35 AUSEST (read-only agent at 35402e4322): HOLDS. invalidate-conflicted-key-fx (mutation_events.cljc :567-585) returns nil for a tagless entry - its own docstring claims the read path will reload on the next ensure, which is false for a still-FRESH entry; settle-optimistic-rollback :586-643 leaves every :invalidate disposition entry untouched, drops the nil fx, and derives :refetched-keys from the disposition name rather than from requests actually enqueued. spec/016 :749 lists :tags among OPTIONAL keys and the conflict-rule table promises stale+refetch under the default policy; note the restore-dangle paragraph (spec/016 ~:1052) already blesses exact-key durable staling in place - shipped prior art for the recommended fix. SURFACES: implementation/resources/** + tests; any spec/016-Resources.md prose alignment is HOT-ZONE spec/* - keep it minimal; no other live/sibling toucher of spec/016, but verify at dispatch time. COLLISIONS: none live (http-after-meta is implementation/http + spec/014) or sibling. GATES: clojure -M:test from implementation/resources (JVM); npm run test:cljs --prefix implementation [HEAVY - shadow compile] for the CLJS arm. AMBIGUITY: recover via the invalidate-tags engine vs direct exact-key staling - follow the bead: mark the exact entry stale with the reply causal time, ordinary refetch only when active owners exist, mirroring the restore-dangle path; and make :reconciliation-refetches name only real requests. SHAPE: solo, first wave.

Therefore an owner-free conflicted key is materially changed (:invalidated-at and :revision advance) but is absent from the mutation instance/failed trace/reply-to :affected-keys. title: surface-review(skill-implementor): make the pinned spec and fixtures the porting loop
description:
## Scope

Rework skills/re-frame2-implementor/** as a compact execution guide for building a minimum second implementation. Preserve the existing eight-host React+VDOM scope, the pinned-spec boundary, spec-gap discipline, and claimed-capability conformance semantics. Replace the current document/session dossier with two things: a short port profile containing only genuine implementor choices, and one repeatable EP loop driven directly by the pinned owning Specs and live conformance fixtures.

The coherent surface includes the published SKILL.md and references, their human/meta docs, the implementor-specific drift guards that currently pin copied prose, and a focused behavioural eval. It does not change the re-frame2 spec, runtime, APIs, capability vocabulary, or fixture corpus.

## Findings

1. The published skill says it routes rather than duplicates the spec, but it has become a second contract. SKILL.md plus the eight shipped reference leaves total 36,816 words / 283,139 characters. phase-2-impl-order.md alone is 15,084 words / 117,782 characters; phase-1-decisions.md is 5,337 words / 44,840 characters. Six of the eight leaves exceed the repository's existing 16 KB leaf ceiling in skills/README.md. A normal Phase-2 session is told to consult the 119 KB EP leaf, often the 28 KB conformance leaf and 25 KB reference tour as well.
2. The skill-internal context-economy claim has drifted from reality. spec/design.md:147-154 says Phase 1 is about 320 lines, a full v1 is about 1,060 lines, and the worst case is comfortably small. The current physical totals are 668 lines for phase-1-decisions.md + decision-record.md and 1,953 lines for SKILL.md + all references, with unusually dense long lines. This is not progressive disclosure when the unit of loading is a whole leaf.
3. Phase 1 records obligations as if they were choices. The kickoff prompt (references/kickoff-prompt.md:24) requires a question for every block, captures every answer, forbids implementation code, and the 254-line decision template requires every placeholder filled and a commit before work (decision-record.md:236-237). Much of D4 is fixed by the spec rather than selected by an implementor: React+VDOM, the JS event loop, no core.async public contract, one frame-state container, closed effect-map policing, structured errors, and the mandatory classification boundary. Reconfirming these in a second document adds ceremony without changing a port.
4. Phase 2 adds project-management policy unrelated to correctness. phase-2-impl-order.md:25 mandates one multi-day EP per focused session and forbids landing two together. output-format.md:31-129 requires Phase-1, per-EP, and v1 report forms; every EP report carries commit hashes, files, tests, fixture lists, carry-over, and a mandatory What surprised me section, while line 131 requires one report per session. A competent implementor should be free to choose commit/session granularity.
5. The feedback loop begins too late. The first full acceptance point comes only after the shared identity/path foundation plus EP 001, 002, 006, views, 009, and 015 (phase-2-impl-order.md:278-294). conformance.md:21 says each host first builds roughly 300 lines of harness, yet harness bootstrap is not an implementation step. The per-EP rule can simply report not run when a fresh port has no script. This allows several multi-day EPs to accumulate before the first objective signal.
6. Verification ownership is internally inconsistent. README.md:26 says compilation, tests, and conformance are the engineer's responsibility; SKILL.md:67, spec/design.md:19,40-62, output-format.md, and skills/README.md:198 say the agent runs a narrow per-EP slice. The full gates are still delegated by default even when the explicitly-invoked, code-writing agent has the tool access to run them.
7. History shows the maintenance cost of copying contract detail. The skill path has been touched by 129 commits since its 2026-05-12 introduction. The shipped router+references grew from about 12,277 words / 90,090 characters at introduction to 36,816 words / 283,139 characters now. Closed beads rf2-ihw9q and rf2-hu5uz show the failure mode directly: the Phase-2 prose pointed a porter at deleted implementation files and a deleted function, while a required checker pinned the dead token, so repairing guidance required coordinated prose/checker surgery.
8. The conformance guidance has strong principles worth preserving—derive tags from the pinned corpus, fail unknown capabilities instead of silently skipping, distinguish spec gaps from port bugs—but its copied catalogues already age. The worked command at conformance.md:183 says 136 fixtures; the current directory contains 245. The harness should enumerate fixture metadata and call/DSL operators at the pin instead of teaching a prose snapshot.
9. Host scope is not the problem. The eight JS-cross-compile-to-React+VDOM hosts and the stop for other hosts match spec/000-Vision.md and spec/Implementor-Checklist.md. Preserve that boundary, but let the checklist own its per-host option matrices instead of restating them in the skill.
10. Evaluation covers discovery only. evals/evals.json:4 explicitly defines trigger-only fixtures; nothing grades whether a TypeScript/Fable port request yields a compact set of decisions, establishes an executable feedback loop, runs the right slice, refuses silent capability skips, or reaches an honest checkpoint. The docs also visibly drift: docs/skills/re-frame2-implementor.md:46 links the current references/ directory through the deleted singular /reference URL.
11. All of this prose ships: package.json:28-33 includes SKILL.md and references/. The internal design/evals are excluded, so they cannot rescue an installed agent from an overlong or stale operational path.

## Recommended Action

Make the pinned spec and fixtures the working loop rather than mirroring them.

1. Replace the 254-line DECISIONS.md dossier with a compact port profile containing only: upstream pin/origin, host/toolchain, genuinely chosen host mechanisms, optional capability claim/known skips, and current conformance score. Fixed pattern obligations are links to their owning Spec, not fields the implementor must copy and reconfirm. For an unqualified minimum-port request, default optional capabilities to no and choose ordinary host-idiomatic mechanisms where repository context makes them clear; ask only for a missing choice that materially changes the implementation.
2. Replace the long kickoff and three report templates with one concise execution contract. Do not mandate a fresh session, per-EP commit, one EP per session, surprise diary, or a committed record before code. A checkpoint should report only changed decisions, code/result, exact test command and outcome, conformance delta, and genuine blockers/spec gaps.
3. Replace the 119 KB Phase-2 contract mirror with a small EP index: dependency order, owning Spec/API/Conventions links, capability family, and prerequisites. Every EP then follows one uniform loop: read the owner at the recorded pin; enumerate applicable fixture ids/capabilities/operators from that same pin; implement the smallest vertical slice; run the narrow slice; repair or diagnose; update the compact profile only if a real choice or claim changed.
4. Bootstrap fixture discovery and the smallest useful harness seam before or alongside the first foundational implementation slice. Grow support for handler-DSL and Mode-B operators only as live fixtures require it, while failing loud on an unknown fixture spec version, capability, DSL op, or call op. Do not invent a generated fixture translation layer or a cross-host compatibility package.
5. Let a tool-capable agent run the port's discovered noninteractive unit/conformance gates, including the full claimed-capability gate when the user asked for an end-to-end implementation. Interactive/visual work can remain a concise programmer handoff when no drivable runtime exists. Use the host agent's normal permissions instead of a skill-local engineer/agent relay policy.
6. Keep the valuable conformance and safety invariants concise and singular: pinned provenance, no silent unknown skips, passed / claimed-applicable, spec-gap-vs-port-bug diagnosis, explicit approval for upstream issue creation, and relevant tooling-security boundaries. Link to the source contract for all framework semantics.
7. Retire or narrow structural checker arms that require copied implementation tokens/paragraphs. Keep focused guards for genuinely load-bearing workflow invariants (foundation ordering, all three required capability families, no bead-id leakage, issue-filing safety), but do not require a second prose rendering of the runtime contract.
8. Add one focused behavioural eval around a small TypeScript-shaped port workspace. It should prove the default minimum-port prompt creates the compact profile without an exhaustive interview, establishes/runs the first real slice, reports observed results, and fails on a controlled wrong implementation or unknown capability. Keep the existing out-of-scope host/substrate negatives. This is one outcome witness, not a general eval platform.
9. Reconcile the published README/docs and internal design claims with the reduced workflow, including the broken references/ link and measured size/load statements.

## Evidence

- Runtime guidance census at current main: SKILL.md + eight references = 36,816 words / 283,139 characters; physical line count = 1,953.
- Largest leaves: references/phase-2-impl-order.md 119,590 bytes; phase-1-decisions.md 46,018; conformance.md 28,495; reference-impl-tour.md 26,306; cardinal-rules.md 21,203; decision-record.md 19,345. The family ceiling is skills/README.md:246-251 (at most 250 lines and 16 KB, one-level routing).
- Stated non-duplication: skills/re-frame2-implementor/README.md:37 and spec/design.md:13. Actual Phase-2 leaf contains 15,084 words of normative contract restatement.
- Ceremony: references/kickoff-prompt.md:24,53; references/decision-record.md:58,236-237; references/phase-2-impl-order.md:25; references/output-format.md:31-131.
- Late feedback and ownership conflict: references/phase-2-impl-order.md:278-294; references/conformance.md:21; README.md:26; SKILL.md:67; skills/README.md:198.
- Trigger-only eval: evals/evals.json:4-26.
- Published package surface: package.json:28-33.
- Drift examples: references/conformance.md:183 versus 245 current fixture files; docs/skills/re-frame2-implementor.md:46 singular-directory URL.
- History: 129 commits touch the skill path since 80ffd92404; initial router+references about 12,277 words / 90,090 characters versus 36,816 / 283,139 now. rf2-ihw9q and rf2-hu5uz document dead worked-example prose pinned by scripts/check_skill_implementor_partition_drift.py.
- Duplicate search: all-status title/description searches for skill-implementor, re-frame2-implementor, decision record, port profile, conformance-first, kickoff prompt, per-EP wrap-up, token burden, and second implementation found no bead owning this outcome.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Given a pinned local spec checkout and an unqualified build a minimum re-frame2 port in TypeScript request, the skill takes no question-per-D-block or question-per-optional-EP interview. It records a compact port profile of actual choices/claims and begins the first implementation/verification slice in the same run; no fixed spec obligation is copied as a confirmation field.
2. The default route needs SKILL.md plus at most one one-level-deep operational leaf to begin work. Shipped leaves obey the existing 16 KB discipline unless a measured catalogue exception demonstrably reduces per-session tokens; the current monolithic Phase-2 leaf is not retained as an exception. Total shipped operational prose is a net material reduction, not the same text redistributed across more files.
3. The port profile contains the spec pin, host/toolchain, material mechanism choices, claimed/known-skipped capability set, fixture-less self-tests where applicable, and latest score. It has no mandatory per-session log, commit hash chain, repeated fixed obligations, or fill every placeholder rule.
4. Each foundational EP checkpoint is driven by current fixture metadata at the pin and reports an exact runnable unit/conformance slice. A fresh port cannot call successive EPs landed solely with no port script yet; the workflow establishes the minimal runner/test seam early and fails loud on unknown spec versions, capabilities, DSL ops, and Mode-B call ops.
5. A tool-capable end-to-end session runs the discovered noninteractive per-EP and full claimed-capability gates itself and reports exact commands, exits, and passed / claimed-applicable. It hands off only unavailable interactive/visual evidence, and never claims completion while that required evidence is pending.
6. The reduced EP index preserves the required order and the three foundation families (:core/*, :identity/*, :data-classification/*), host scope, spec-authority rule, no-silent-skip rule, and spec-gap approval boundary. Framework contract detail remains owned by the pinned Specs/fixtures rather than duplicated in the skill.
7. One focused checked-in behavioural eval exercises the minimum TypeScript path through compact profiling and a real first slice. A controlled bad implementation or unknown-capability mutation makes it fail, proving the signal is non-vacuous. Existing trigger routing still sends out-of-scope hosts/substrates and application-authoring requests elsewhere.
8. Implementor-specific drift checks are updated in the same change: obsolete literal-prose/token locks are retired or narrowed with self-tests, while remaining workflow/safety invariants stay enforced. No new generated manifest, prose synchronizer, or copied contract catalogue is introduced.
9. README.md, docs/skills/re-frame2-implementor.md, package/plugin metadata, and spec/{design,inputs,authoring-prompt}.md describe the same compact workflow, current verification ownership, and actual load shape; the broken references/ URL is fixed.
10. The PR reports before/after word/byte load for the default route, the behavioural eval result, focused drift-guard results, package contents, and link checks.

## Non-goals

- No change to re-frame2 framework semantics, API, capability tags, fixture expectations, eight-host scope, or React+VDOM boundary.
- No TypeScript reference implementation, second maintained runtime, cross-host compatibility layer, generated fixture translation, or generic conformance package.
- No new decision schema, progress database, report generator, session orchestrator, mandatory commit convention, or compatibility support for the old DECISIONS.md/report shapes.
- No exhaustive per-host recipe matrix or additional cardinal-rule prose; the Implementor Checklist and owning Specs retain those details.
- No weakening of conformance scoring, unknown-capability failure, spec-version checks, data-classification coverage, tooling security, or per-issue approval for upstream GitHub writes.
- No requirement to finish an entire second implementation inside the behavioural eval; the witness only needs to prove the compact start and first real feedback slice.
- No rewrite of sibling skills or the global skill routing taxonomy.

## Related beads

- rf2-ihw9q and rf2-hu5uz (closed) are direct historical evidence that copied Phase-2 implementation detail plus literal-token guards can preserve stale porting guidance.
- rf2-g9k0g (open) independently gives the application-authoring skill a closed verification loop; this task applies the same trust-the-explicit-invoker principle to a different product while retaining implementor-specific conformance.
- rf2-rc0yh (open) independently collapses the setup skill to one runnable default and a behavioural witness; coordinate only on shared skills/README.md policy wording.
- rf2-8jwb7 (open) independently removes migration paste-loop ceremony; coordinate only if verification-posture wording is edited concurrently.
- No existing open, deferred, or closed bead owns this implementor-skill profile/fixture-loop reduction.

description: PR #10041 adds a 2000ms cancelled retention window, but machine_after_rings_helpers/needs-ticking? still returns false when only cancelled timers remain. overlay-tree kicks only when that predicate passes; tick-loop! publishes at most its final tick then stops. PR **#10112** merged by rebase at head `dea0ecd656de57a39571926ac9c1fb9bf6caa77a`; merge commit
`3c912a0aea`. Trunk `2ecf003d11` -> `3c912a0aea`; `HEAD` == `origin/main` after the fast-forward, two
separate reads. **5 files, 403 insertions / 23 deletions**, the bulk of it a 259-line regression.

**Five clauses:** rollup **88** at band; failed **0**, pending **0**, case-folded and status-gated
(**53 skipped + 35 success**); **4** runs (portability, docs, lint, tests) all `completed`/`success`,
**0** not completed, oid at the full 40 characters and the run list non-empty; matrix control
self-derived, `LAST` = `b9220b6dc2ea`, **1** then **0**, ancestry confirmed.

**Direction test:** merge-base `377dd940fa65`, trunk-side **6**, branch-side **5**, **overlap 0**,
`merge-tree --write-tree` exit **0**. Neither live worker's surface is touched.

**Not reopened**; appended. **Refused once before merging**, at total 87 / pending 2 with `tests`
in_progress — clause 3 — then re-verified in full at the point of merge rather than on the waiter's read.

**THE MAYOR VERIFIED THE STRUCTURE, NOT THE DIFF.** `cancelled-ring-live?` is defined at
`machine_after_rings_helpers.cljc:365` and is read from **exactly two places**: the prune/expiry path at
`:455` and inside `needs-ticking?` at `:692`. **So "this ring is still visible" and "the clock still
owes this ring a tick" are now ONE predicate and cannot drift apart** — which is the whole of the fix,
and it is a structural property rather than two constants that happen to agree. `needs-ticking?` sits at
`:659` and is 3-arity; both call sites pass three arguments, at `machine_after_rings.cljs:448` and
`:595`. **The arity widening is the load-bearing choice**: a missed call site is now a compile error
rather than a silent survivor holding the old 2-arity behaviour.

**THE SHAPE CHOSEN WAS THE CHEAP ONE, AND THE REASONING IS WHY IT IS RIGHT.** Keep the existing clock
alive until pending cancellations expire — NOT a per-deadline refresh. Both call sites *already* pruned
against the same `now` they now pass the predicate, so the widened gate reads the very instant the
vector was pruned at: **no new clock, no new scheduling mechanism, no per-ring and no per-record
timer.** Lock #8 survives — one clock per chart, `O(charts)` not `O(rings x charts)` — and **the clock
still stops**, bounded, outliving the last armed timer by at most `cancelled-retention-ms` (2000).

**THE CLAIM UNDER TEST WAS MADE TRUE AND KEPT AS HISTORY — this is the best handling of one this
session.** The old docstring read *"There are no armed timers (`:cancelled` rings are static)"*. It now
states the rule that actually holds, and then quotes the old text and names the cause: *"rf2-q9x6h —
this used to read \\"there are no armed timers (`:cancelled` rings are static)\\", and `:cancelled` rings

description: PR #10020 fixes filtered-empty navigation, but its claim that the shared helper uses the same domain as compose-focus/focus-step-reducer is false when the stored focus has no frame restriction. shell/nav-boundary-state filters raw bundles by (:frame focus) from the COMPOSED :rf.xray/focus. compose-focus resolves that field to the current row's frame even when the stored [:focus :frame] is nil. Preserve the filtered-empty fix and explicit picker scope. Add a regression comparing the boundary with the real step reducer for an unscoped cross-frame sequence and its explicitly scoped control. No new navigation mode or public API is requested. No exact open finding exists.

title: Incomplete HTTP wire-vocabulary CI coverage: HTTP-only diffs skip the emitter gate
description:
Discovered while auditing merged PR #9897 (08f046f0f7a1efc879a5435f1715040e7b28c60f). The source Bead notes explicitly reported this coverage gap, but no open Bead records its correction. This is an existing CI gap exposed by the review, not a claim that #9897 itself skipped the gate: its core-test edit armed the broader lane.

Evidence: tools/mcp-conformance/wire-vocab/test/re_frame/mcp_conformance/trace_catalogue_lint_test.clj:48 and reply_envelope_test.clj:217 both roster implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/transport.cljc (the trace catalogue also rosters registry.cljc). .github/workflows/test.yml:6130 runs mcp-conformance-wire-vocab only when mcp_conformance is true. Invoking the absolute classifier with only implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/transport.cljc returned exit 0, implementation_jvm=true, mcp_conformance=false. The same invocation with implementation/core/src/re_frame/fx.cljc returned exit 0 and mcp_conformance=true. Therefore an HTTP-only change can regress a pinned reply-envelope/trace vocabulary and still skip its existing checking job.

Correction: connect the existing HTTP emitter inputs to the existing wire-vocab gate through the smallest appropriate classifier change, and pin the classification with a representative HTTP-only input and a negative control. Do not add a new gate or a general dependency graph. Preserve unrelated heavy-lane scoping.

Acceptance: a diff confined to a rostered HTTP emitter schedules the gate that reads it; the existing classifier regression suite demonstrates this, and the wire-vocab suite still passes. Record the actual HTTP-only output, not an all-surfaces or core-inclusive diff.
notes: Merged-PR audit #9993 (3b28b0653bea33d3f783217e85c591f1a43e5831; merged 2026-09-17T20:21:37Z). Completeness: Adds the HTTP source-to-conformance edge and pins both rostered emitters, directory coverage, existing fan-out and excluded tests/deps/live lane. Correctness: Both conformance suites explicitly read the HTTP source paths. The new nested src pattern adds only mcp_conformance inside the existing per-feature branch; source/test and sibling negative controls match that scope. Full classifier and regression diff reviewed; no local suite run. Implementation quality: Reuses the existing gate and directory-level classifier without a second production roster or dependency service; no actionable finding. Actionable findings: none. Existing finding updates: none.

title: review(xray/shell-spine): senior-developer findings, 10 ranked, 5 spec chapters drift, trunk 9555881fe3 (2026-09-17)
description:
# Senior review: xray-shell-spine

Reviewer persona: senior front-end engineer who has shipped devtools UIs (browser devtools panels, editor extensions); judges a tool by whether the thing you came for is one keystroke away and whether focus, selection and navigation state can ever desynchronise.
Tree: xray-review-sep17 worktree, trunk 9555881fe3
Scope read: tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/{shell.cljs (3380, in full), spine.cljs (1229), spine_filters.cljs (780), focus.cljc (369), frame_switcher.cljs (637), keybinding.cljs (602), resize_handle.cljs (896), panels.cljs (861), panel_registry.cljc (188), panel_enum.cljc (138)} = 9,080 lines; plus the handlers they lean on in registry.cljs, epoch.cljs, filters.cljs, mount.cljs, settings/view.cljs, palette/subs.cljs, static/shell.cljs. Tests skimmed for what is pinned: shell_cljs_test, spine_cljs_test, focus_cljs_test, focus_host_frame_async_*_test, frame_switcher_cljs_test, keybinding_cljs_test, mount_cljs_test, panels_mount_cljs_test, registry_cljs_test, app_db_diff_cljs_test, panels_e2e/multi_frame_isolation_e2e_cljs_test.
Owning specs consulted (each end to end): tools/xray/spec/007-UX-IA.md, 018-Event-Spine.md, 012-Views.md, 011-Launch-Modes.md, DESIGN-RATIONALE.md (Locks #7, #9, #14, #15, #17).

## Findings, ranked

### 1. Every spine key (j / k / L / Shift+G / , / s) goes dead the moment DOM focus sits on a row or a ribbon button  [CONFIRMED] [severity: high] [kind: ergonomics] [size: S]
- Where: tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/keybinding.cljs:485-498 (the `:else` arm), :237-256 (`target-activatable?`); tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/shell.cljs:1772-1773 (rows are `role="button"` + `tab-index "0"`), :952-975 (nav chevrons are `<button>`s).
- What: `target-activatable?` was added (rf2-d716o9) so Space yields to a focused `<button>`/`<summary>`/`[role=button]`, but it is `and`-ed in front of `spine-key-id` for the WHOLE roster, so after the most natural gesture in the tool (click an L2 row, or click `‹`/`›`) the focused element swallows j / k / L / Shift+G / `,` / `s` until the user clicks somewhere inert.
- Evidence: `:else` arm reads `(and (shell-visible?) (target-inside-xray? e) (not (target-editable? e)) (not (target-activatable? e)) (not (target-inside-modal? e)))` around `(spine-key-id e)`; the exemption is not scoped to Space. Rows: shell.cljs:1772 `:role "button"`, :1773 `:tab-index "0"`; the row's own `:on-key-down` (:1780-1813) handles only Enter / Space / ContextMenu / Shift+F10, so j/k reach neither handler. Browsers focus a `tabindex=0` element on mousedown, so this is the post-click state. Control: keybinding_cljs_test.cljs:854-950 pins Space on BUTTON/SUMMARY/role=button (yields) and Space on DIV (fires); no test in that file sends `j`/`k` at an activatable target (pattern `KeyJ|"j"` hits only roster tests on inert targets). 007-UX-IA.md:1204-1214 does document the guard as roster-wide, so 007 matches the code; 018-Event-Spine.md:1760-1763 lists j/k/L with no carve-out. Neither the code nor 007 is right: only Space (and Enter, which is not a spine key) is consumed by a native control.
- Action: narrow to `(and (target-activatable? e) (space-key? e))` and add one test row (bare `j` on a `role=button` target inside the shell dispatches `:rf.xray/focus-event-prev`); trim the 007:1204-1214 sentence to say Space.

### 2. Cold start: L2 highlights the head row while the Epoch panel says "No event focused" — until the user clicks something  [CONFIRMED] [severity: high] [kind: correctness] [size: S]
- Where: tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/epoch.cljs:135-141 (`:rf.xray/epoch-recorded` no-ops unless `frame-id = target`); mount.cljs:780-803 (`::seed-trace-and-target-frame` seeds nil when no cascade precedes first mount); spine.cljs:515-521 (`eff-epoch-id` derived only from the `:epoch-history` slot); frame_switcher.cljs:557-562, :349 (`view-scope-frame` and the picker face fall back to the head frame); panels/epoch/view.cljs:6121 (the empty-state string).
- What: when Xray mounts before the host's first cascade (preload `boot-on-runtime-ready!`, any app whose first dispatch is user-driven — the two_frame_isolation and standard_epochs testbeds are exactly this), `:target-frame` is nil and stays nil: `:rf.xray/epoch-recorded` compares every recording frame against nil and drops it, so `:epoch-history` never fills, `compose-focus` yields `:epoch-id nil`, and the L4 Epoch panel (Lock #7's hero) renders "No event focused. Click an event in the list to inspect its pipeline." while the L2 list fills, LIVE auto-follow highlights the head row, and the Frame picker face shows that row's frame as if selected.
- Evidence: the only writers of `:target-frame` are epoch.cljs:116 (`set-target-frame`, called from mount seed and `core/set-target-frame!`), spine.cljs:832 (`set-frame-reducer`, picker) and spine.cljs:913 (`reseed-epoch-history-for-frame`, called from focus-event / prev / next / focus-epoch / select-dispatch-id) — grep `assoc :target-frame|assoc db :target-frame` over src, 3 hits, all read; nothing on the trace-ingest path adopts a frame. EP-0002 (rf2-bd4div, pinned at mount_cljs_test.cljs:1200-1215 and panels_mount_cljs_test.cljs:782-799) rules only that nil must not be repaired to a synthesised `:rf/default`; it says "the frame picker prompts a choice", but frame_switcher.cljs:349 `(or selected-frame (first frames))` shows the head frame, so nothing prompts. registry_cljs_test.cljs:2193-2201 pins the non-target drop; no test pins what happens to a nil target when a real frame records (grep `epoch-recorded` in test/: 11 files, none with a nil target followed by a recording frame).
- Action: in `:rf.xray/epoch-recorded`, when `(:target-frame db)` is nil adopt `frame-id` (assoc `:target-frame` + `[:focus :frame]`, exactly what `set-target-frame` does for a non-nil id). It is not `:rf/default` synthesis — the frame recorded — and `view-scope-frame` reads `target-slot` before its head fallback, so L2 and L4 agree by construction afterwards. One test: nil target, `epoch-recorded :above` → target `:above`, history non-empty.

### 3. Nothing in the Dynamic chrome tells you whether you are LIVE, pinned (RETRO) or paused  [CONFIRMED] [severity: high] [kind: ergonomics] [size: M]
- Where: tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/shell.cljs:27-31 (ns docstring: mode pill dropped rf2-g9pee "relying on row cues"), :1295-1301 (stripe retired rf2-4yemd), :1198-1228 (`nav-boundary-state` computes `:live?` — consumed only to disable `»`), :1631-1955 (`event-row` — no live/retro/paused class or glyph), :2219-2303 (`event-list-tree`).
- What: the spine has three states the user must know to read a panel (LIVE auto-follow, RETRO pin, LIVE-paused via Space), and the only visible difference between them is whether the `»` chevron is disabled; the mode pill (rf2-g9pee) and the head-row pulse/gutter cues (rf2-pjjwh) were each removed on the assumption the other carried the signal.
- Evidence: grep `stale\?|pulse|"LIVE"|"RETRO"` in shell.cljs: one comment hit (:3326), no code; the only `:paused?` reads are :1207/:1225 (nav boundary) and :2242-2244 (auto-scroll gating); control `No events.` at :2276 and `focused?` :1683 found. `event_status_colour.cljc:312-316` computes `:stale?`/`:paused?`/`:mode` per row, but shell.cljs never turns them into a class or glyph. Spec promises: 007-UX-IA.md:158-163, :489, :1180-1191 (LIVE pulse on the head row, motion spec), 018-Event-Spine.md:249-257 (head-row pulse cue), :1132-1133; DESIGN-RATIONALE.md Lock #14 :500-624 (two-segment mode pill, signal #3 LIVE pulse). Every one describes a cue the code no longer paints.
- Action: decide: A) re-add one cheap cue — a `data-rf-xray-mode` attribute on the L2 `<ul>` plus a 2px left rule colour (violet LIVE / cyan RETRO / grey paused) — and rewrite 007/018/DR to that; or B) keep the chrome bare and strike the three spec passages. A is a morning; B is a spec edit. Either closes the drift.

### 4. `:rf.xray/focus-epoch` fallback pins `:epoch-id` in RETRO but leaves the old `:dispatch-id`, so the L2 highlight and L4 disagree  [CONFIRMED] [severity: medium] [kind: correctness] [size: S]

title: fresco: two silent seam drops — React's missing-key warning at every boundary crossing, and an h/event intent inside a key map (rf2-pk4i6 item 16)
description:
Shortlist item 16 of the rf2-pk4i6 senior-review wave (from rf2-pk4i6.6#1 and rf2-pk4i6.6#2). Mike ruled the whole shortlist as actioned; this is the filed follow-on. Size S. One artefact, one PR.

## Two seams, and they fail in the same register: SILENTLY

**Seam 1 — React's missing-key warning is lost at every boundary crossing.** An unkeyed `(for …)` handed to a `defview` / `error-boundary` / `overlay` as children is spliced into separate `createElement` arguments, which React marks validated and therefore never key-checks. So an unkeyed list of memoised boundaries reconciles BY INDEX in silence: delete row 0 and every row's local state is handed the next row's data.

**Seam 2 — an `h/event` inside a key map has its intent dropped.** `{"Enter" (h/event [e] … [:form/commit])}` takes the `(fn? v)` arm, so the vector it returns is ignored. No error, no dispatch — against the `event` docstring's promise, which holds at every `on*`-spelled position.

## The triage's citations (claims, to be opened at tip before editing)

- `check-seq-keys!` — `implementation/fresco/src/re_frame/fresco/impl/codec.cljs`, the crossing loop.
- `key-map-handler` and `event-callback` — `implementation/fresco/src/re_frame/fresco/impl/intent.cljs`.
- `codec_cljs_test.cljs:1206` — where the `[view {} (for …)]` case belongs.
- `intent_cljs_test.cljs:384` — where the key-map row belongs.

Re-verified by the reviewer: NO. Both are line-cited with the pinned-versus-unpinned cases named, and the reviewer judged the test rows the cheap confirmation. So the test rows are the first thing to write, not the last.

## What the triage proposes (a proposal, verified before obeyed)

- In `check-seq-keys!`'s crossing loop, warn ONCE PER SITE when a boundary-headed member has no `:key`, under the EXISTING `keywarn` dedupe and the EXISTING `goog.DEBUG` gate. Both already exist — use them; do not add a second dedupe or a second gate.
- Add `(callback? v) (event-callback k v)` AHEAD of the `(fn? v)` arm in `key-map-handler`. Three lines.

## The scope limit is part of the item

One artefact, one PR. This is not a licence to rework Fresco's key handling or its intent dispatch. `goog.DEBUG` means the key warning costs production nothing, and the stance applies directly: trust the programmer, warn once, do not nag.

## Surface and fences

Yours: `implementation/fresco/src/**` (notably `impl/codec.cljs` and `impl/intent.cljs`) and `implementation/fresco/test/**`.

**No live worker touches Fresco**, so this artefact is yours alone.

Not yours: `implementation/core/**`, `implementation/epoch/**` and `spec/002` (a worker is live there); `implementation/resources/**` and `spec/016` (a worker is live there); `implementation/http/**` and `spec/014` (a worker is live there); `spec/001` and `core.cljc` (a worker is live there). `spec/006` is hot-zone and shortlist item 8 is queued against it — do not edit it; report if you believe it needs a sentence. `spec/API.md` and its manifest sidecars are hot-zone: report, do not edit.

## Worker verdict (2026-09-16) — PR #9898, both seams fixed

BOTH PREMISES HELD. Verified by writing the failing rows first, against the
unfixed tree, before any source edit.

Seam 1 (missing key lost at the crossing): CONFIRMED. `check-member-key!`
only ever warned on a `:key` that was PRESENT and entity-valued; an absent
key was left to React by an explicit decision, recorded in a comment and
pinned by a passing test. That decision is correct under a HOST parent and
wrong at a boundary crossing, which is the distinction the code did not draw.

Seam 2 (callback in a key map): CONFIRMED. `key-map-handler` classified with
`fn?` before `callback?`, and `callback?` IS `fn?` plus a marker read, so the
callback took the plain-function arm and its returned intent was dropped.

### One correction to the triage's stated mechanism

The bead says the crossing splices members "into separate createElement
arguments, which React marks validated". That is true of what the BODY later
does with them, not of `boundary-element` itself: `boundary-element` passes
NO child arguments to createElement at all — the flattened children ride
inside `rfProps` as CLJS data. So React is not merely failing to check them,
it never receives them as children. The conclusion is unchanged and the fix
location (`check-seq-keys!`) is right; only the description was imprecise.

### Finding that governs how future Fresco key tests are written

REACT 19 REMOVED KEY VALIDATION FROM `createElement` — the reconciler does it
during render. Measured on react@19.3.0 with a console.error spy over an array
child: zero errors. So at `as-element` time React is silent about EVERY shape,
keyed or not, host parent or boundary.

Consequence: any row asserting "React said nothing here" passes on a fully
fixed tree and on a completely broken one alike — a vacuous green. A first
draft of this work contained exactly such a row, with a host-parent control
that was expected to bite and did not. It was removed rather than shipped.
The mechanism is now pinned STRUCTURALLY instead: under a host parent the seq
arrives as a React children array; at the crossing there is no children slot
at all. That is measurable in this lane and is not vacuous.

This also makes the pre-existing comment "React already warns about a missing
key" stale at element-creation time. It remains true at RENDER time, which is
why the host-parent path is still left to React; the comment was reworded to
say when.
