      the population U4 is stated over. Same window! mechanism, but an estimator over FRAME
      INTERVALS rather than over window lengths. Worth its own bead.
  (b) A SUITE-LEVEL SELF-TEST. The sibling driver has slice_echo_window_dom_cljs_test.cljs; this
      one has none. It carries six instrument-integrity controls that run IN the driver (a
      canonical-DOM parity gate with its own negative control, four echo negative controls, the
      tally, the guard and the additive positive control), which is the stronger place by the
      sibling's own argument -- but a browser-suite row proving the repairs is still owed.
  (c) THE WINDOW ITSELF, for U3/C3/C4, on a quiet box. Note the resolution caveat the driver
      publishes: a paint-bounded window is dominated by the frame grid, so :over-floor's
      :straddles-1? must be read on each measured arm BEFORE any :comparative range is quoted.
      If the shipped seed cannot separate the measured arms from an empty frame, the honest
      conclusion is that C3 needs a BROADER POPULATION than the slice's feed page -- a finding
      about the row, never a licence to widen a band.

GATES. npm run test:hicasso-compile is the gate covering this surface; it is heavyweight and was
NOT run locally (loud box), but it auto-covers new files by walking the lane directory and runs
on every PR in test.yml, so CI gates the compile. Locally: a Clojure-aware delimiter-balance check
and a qualified-reference resolution check (45 refs in the driver, 8 in the donor views, all
resolve), each with a planted-fault discrimination proof and a restore verified by blob hash.
U4's half is now filed separately as rf2-xc0bw (a per-frame driver on the LEDGER witness, edit-shaped and loud-box-safe). This bead keeps items (b) the suite-level self-test and (c) the quiet-box window for U3/C3/C4.
AUDIT OF PR #8599 (2026-08-21) — repair before the quiet-box U3/C3/C4 window.

Two measurement-fidelity defects belong to this existing owner; no duplicate bead was created.

1. DONOR FEED READ-SET IS LARGER ON THE SHIPPED POPULATION. slice_donor_views.cljs feed-page always calls use-subscribe for [::subs/t :feed/empty], while the Hicasso feed-page calls h/sub for that value only in its empty branch. The pinned seed is non-empty, so the donor locale arm carries an extra subscription/hook that the Hicasso locale arm does not. That adds work to the denominator and can flatter the C3 Hicasso/UIx ratio. Keep the branch-local read branch-local (for example via an empty-state child boundary) and make the suite self-test prove the relevant read roster, not only canonical DOM.

2. THE THEME ARMS RUN OVER DIFFERENT LOCALE-STATE MIXES. :locale and :ctl-blocked both toggle the shared Hicasso frame's locale, while only :donor-locale toggles the donor frame. Replaying the six-arm lane/slot-order at measured slots s=8..19 shows :theme runs in the non-seed locale on 4/12 visits per round, but :donor-theme does so on 8/12. Thus the comparative theme medians are drawn from different page-state populations; the seeded-only canonical parity gate cannot see the divergence after sampling begins. Isolate the control's state/root or deterministically establish each arm's pre-state, and add a schedule-level self-test that proves paired arms see the same governed state mix.
AUDIT REPAIRS 1 AND 2 PLUS ITEM (b) LANDED in PR #8606 (worker/echoself-9wmqd, 2026-08-21). NO WINDOW AND NO BENCH RUN WAS TAKEN; no ledger cell moves; no threshold, band or gate created. ITEM (c) IS UNTOUCHED and this bead stays OPEN on it.

BOTH PREMISES RE-VERIFIED AT SOURCE, both held. slice_donor_views.cljs feed-page bound empty-label unconditionally in its let; slice/views.cljs feed-page reads [::subs/t :feed/empty] only inside its empty branch; the seed is seven articles at a page size of three, so the branch never renders.

THE 4/12 AND 8/12 COUNTS REPRODUCED EXACTLY, in every one of the five rounds. Replaying the six-arm lane/visit-plan (order_guard/slot-order rotate-then-reflect at k=6, indexed by the SAMPLE index, not by the round) at {:warmup 8 :samples 12} over 5 rounds: at measured slots s=8..19, :theme runs in the non-seed locale on 4/12 visits per round and :donor-theme on 8/12.

THE SAME REPLAY FOUND A SECOND DIVERGENCE THE AUDIT DID NOT NAME, in the other dimension and on the POSITIVE CONTROL'S pairing: :ctl-blocked runs in the non-seed THEME on 8/12 measured visits per round against :locale's 4/12, and control-per-round subtracts those two medians. Same mechanism, same class. Both are closed.

WHAT LANDED.
1. Repair 1 on the DONOR SIDE only (slice/views.cljs is a shipped example consumed by a11y/l0/l2 tests): an empty-state child boundary, feed-empty, which costs the measured population nothing because its branch never renders at the seed. The full read roster was then swept boundary by boundary and the result recorded in the donor namespace docstring: chrome 7/7, article-row 2/2, digest 5/5, digest-body/callout/unsupported 1/1 each, pager 5/5 at the seed, app 4 against 3. TWO other differences exist and neither is the same defect. The PAGER is a source-located REFUSAL: the same child-boundary repair would put an extra boundary on the MEASURED page (the seed always renders a pager), which is the same error in the same direction, larger and always on. The shell's missing [:rf.route/id] read runs in the DENOMINATOR'S favour.
2. Repair 2 by ESTABLISHING each arm's pre-state, not by isolating the control. Arms declare :side and :alternates; pre-state is a pure fn of the arm and its own visit index; establish-pre-state! moves the frame through the application's own events, outside every window, on parity-discrimination!'s door and settle. Paired arms then see identical mixes at EVERY schedule by construction.
   WHY THE OTHER CANDIDATE WAS REJECTED, on a replay rather than on taste: both isolating variants (control restores its locale / control on its own root) equalise the theme pair at {8,12} and STOP DOING SO at {8,13} and {8,20} -- the equality is an accident of how slot-order's rotation lands on twelve indices, and sampling's own docstring says the run reading this instrument will raise those counts. The own-root variant also leaves the control's own theme mix wrong (0/12 against 4/12).
3. Item (b): implementation/hicasso/test/re_frame/bench/hicasso/slice_broad_window_dom_cljs_test.cljs, beside slice_broad_clock_app.cljs (the driver both repairs live in; the sibling slice_echo_clock_app already has its own suite). Ten rows.

WHAT THE SELF-TEST PROVES, beyond canonical DOM -- both first-class, each with its own negative control.
- READ ROSTER: both frames' subscription caches through subs.tooling/sub-cache-snapshot (the same per-frame cache BOTH substrates go through -- Hicasso's collector calls subs/subscribe for every h/sub edge, the UIx adapter for every hook). Asserts donor-minus-hicasso is EMPTY, [::subs/t :feed/empty] is in NEITHER, [:rf.route/id] is hicasso-only, with anti-vacuity first. NEGATIVE CONTROL re-plants exactly the removed read as a UIx boundary on the donor frame in its own root and requires the comparison to go from empty to naming exactly that read.
- GOVERNED STATE MIX: replays lane/visit-plan through the driver's own pre-state and asserts the three compared pairs are one population at five schedules including {8,13} and {8,20}. NEGATIVE CONTROL models the rig PR #8599 shipped and requires the same comparison to refuse, reproducing 4-against-8 on the locale dimension and 8-against-4 on the control's theme dimension INSIDE the suite, then shows the repaired model passing at the same schedule.
- AND A BRIDGE from the arithmetic to the instrument, because a pure replay proves a model rather than a driver: one DOM row calls establish-pre-state! for both parities on both frames and reads the result back through the driver's own echo checks; another runs a tiny schedule end to end and asserts each arm's visit counter advanced exactly once per planned visit.

NO SEVENTH IN-DRIVER CONTROL WAS ADDED. The driver already runs six and in-driver is the stronger place; what was missing was the browser-suite row.

WHAT THE SUITE DELIBERATELY DOES NOT RE-ADJUDICATE, stated in the file: the canonical-DOM parity gate is a RELEASE gate by construction (data-rf2-source-coord makes the two arms' attributes differ under goog.DEBUG), so a dev-compiled row asserting that equality would either fail honestly or have to strip attributes until it passed.

GATES. npm run test:hicasso-compile covers this surface and auto-covers the new file by walking the lane directory; it was NOT run locally (a peer worker held a live allocation window on the box and two heavyweight runs wedge rather than fail), and CI gates the compile. No fast-PR spine, no shadow-cljs, no browser run. Locally: a Clojure-aware delimiter-balance check and a qualified-reference resolution check over all three files -- 98 distinct in-repo refs (45 driver / 20 donor views / 33 suite), 0 unresolved, 8 further refs external and reported as out of reach rather than counted. Three planted faults, one per file, each red naming what was planted, each restore verified by identical blob hash against the committed object. Re-run green on the final base after a rebase past twelve landings. implementation/package.json was NOT touched: -dom-cljs-test$ is discovered by ns-regexp and needs no registration.
CI CYCLE 2 on PR #8606 — the browser lane read the first cut as 14 failures, ONE CAUSE plus one contract bug. Now GREEN on browser-test, node-test and every other check, on a rebased base. No assertion was weakened; one was added.

THE CAUSE, source-located. collector/!cells is a PROCESS-GLOBAL table keyed by (frame, query), and its own comment states that isolation between roots is a property of that keying rather than anything React provides. invalidate-cell! is the repair for a cell whose reaction has been retired -- including, in its own words, 'across a same-id reincarnation' -- but that repair rides the reaction's DISPOSAL HOOK, and make-reset-runtime-fixture retires a frame by resetting frame/frames to {} rather than through it. A second mount on a used frame id therefore finds a live cell holding a dead reaction: subs/subscribe is never called again (empty sub-cache) and no watch is installed (no re-render). THE FIRST RENDER IS PERFECT, which is what makes it silent.

THE EVIDENCE FIT THAT SHAPE EXACTLY: the mount row (1st mount) PASSED and every row after it failed. hic roster #{} against the donor's 34; every Hicasso-side locale/theme pre-state stayed English/light; the tally read 9 unverified of 18 -- precisely the nine Hicasso-side windows, with all six donor-side ones verified.

THE ACT-ENVIRONMENT HYPOTHESIS WAS TESTED AND REJECTED rather than assumed: every 'not wrapped in act(...)' line in that log is timestamped +12.32s / +14.36s and this namespace ran at +28.58s. Neighbouring-suite noise.

THE FIX is the discipline slice-echo-window-dom-cljs-test already keeps. boot! takes the frame ids as an argument (hicasso-frame / donor-frame become documented DEFAULTS for the bench page's single mount); a new frames reader publishes the live pair; frame-for and parity-discrimination! resolve through it, because a caller that dispatched into the default while the page rendered from a fresh id would be writing to a frame nothing reads. The suite mints a fresh pair per row. Mechanism + measurement recorded at source in boot!'s new section MOUNTING TWICE, and in teardown!, which states that it cannot fix this and why.

A REAL CONTRACT BUG THE SUITE ALSO CAUGHT: visits published the last visit INDEX under a docstring promising a COUNT, so it read one short of lane/visit-plan's per-arm count. claim-visit! now banks the count and answers the index. The bridge row earned its place on its first run.

AND THE FIRST DIRECT MEASUREMENT OF THE DONOR'S READ ROSTER, handed over by the empty-Hicasso failure: 34 query vectors, every one of them also read by the Hicasso arm, the fifteen ::subs/t strings matching one for one against the boundary-by-boundary sweep. [::subs/t :feed/empty] is ABSENT -- repair 1 confirmed on the shipped population rather than argued. The roster also reaches a :<- sub's INPUTS and not only the values a body asks for ([:rf.route/query] and [:rf/route] arrive as [::subs/page]'s input chain), which makes the comparison stronger than claimed; the docstring now says so and a new assertion pins it.

THE GREEN IS NOT VACUOUS: the red and green runs both report 1044 tests, and assertions go 5937 -> 5938 -- exactly the one assertion added. Had the DOM rows collapsed to their off-browser skips the count would have dropped by roughly forty-five.

GATES. npm run test:hicasso-compile still NOT run locally (machine contention: a peer held an allocation window throughout), and CI decided it. Browser-test is now a gate that RAN rather than one that was cited: red 14, then green, then green again post-rebase. Local static checks re-run on the final base: 97 distinct in-repo refs, 0 unresolved, exit 0; two further planted faults on this round's own edited lines, each red naming the plant, each restored to an identical blob hash.

ITEM (c) REMAINS UNTOUCHED AND THIS BEAD STAYS OPEN ON IT. No window was run, no reading taken, no ledger cell moved, no threshold, band or gate created.

audit) depends on this bead and cannot close until it does. Its other blocker, rf2-hic-088, is
already CLOSED (PR #8568), so rf2-hic-090 is now the LAST thing standing between rf2-t32wg and

--- ORIGINAL DESCRIPTION FOLLOWS ---

# hic-090 â€” Post-rename recertification

**Phase**: 6 Â· **Est.**: M Â· **Depends**: hic-066
**Surface**: re-run roster + results record (new file); re-runs existing gates, edits nothing

## Goal
A repo-wide rename can change bundle bytes, source coordinates, macro output, and server bytes. Tests and greps are not enough. This bead re-certifies the evidence after hic-066 (and re-runs after any asynchronous override sweep).

## Deliverables
Re-run and record: bundle-isolation/rent sentinels (interpreted-only zero-rent), SSR server bytes + hydration witnesses, native macro-expansion parity, source-coordinate capture (error shapes still point at real locations), and the pinned regression gate.

## Acceptance
All five families green post-sweep; any red is filed in the hic-073 ledger and blocks the release tail per hic-064's green definition.

---
[Worker context â€” applies to every hic bead]
PATH MAP: the normative documents are published in-tree by bead rf2-hic-000:
- docs/design/hicasso/product/decision-brief.md  (= synth.md / "the decision brief")
- docs/design/hicasso/product/specification.md   (= "spec SN" / synth-codex.md)
- docs/design/hicasso/product/lanes/<name>.md    (= codex/<name>.md)
References to `fable/...` are operator-local provenance; workers do not need them.
PROPOSED-ID MAP: "hic-NNN" in any bead text = tracker id rf2-hic-NNN. The dependency manifest is authoritative over prose Depends lines.
WORKER PROTOCOL (mandatory):
1. Run the worker worktree guard before edits: sh scripts/assert-worker-worktree.sh; report WORKTREE_ROOT.
2. Read first: the path-mapped documents this bead names.
3. Gates: foreground a gate that fits inside the harness ceiling; DETACH one that does not and poll BOTH its log and its `.exit` file in a bounded loop within the same turn â€” never end the turn waiting for a completion event. Never pipe a gate through `tail` or any filter; redirect to a log and echo the runner's own exit code on the same command line. Commit and open the PR before ending the turn. DOC-SURFACE GATE: for an edit confined to docs/design/hicasso/, `mkdocs build --strict` is NOT the gate â€” mkdocs.yml's exclude_docs keeps that tree out of the site. `scripts/check_doc_slugs.py` validates its markdown link targets and heading anchors, and `scripts/check_provenance_pins.py` validates changed pages under docs/design/hicasso/; nothing validates its tables, rendering or nav, so verify anchors and table column counts BY HAND and say so in the PR body.
4. Never `git stash`. Commit first, then rebase.
5. Never commit `.beads/issues.jsonl` or `.beads/metadata.json` from a worker branch â€” they are whole-database EXPORTS, not database files, and your branch carries the snapshot taken when its worktree was created, so committing one TIME-TRAVELS the tracker: beads closed since reopen, beads filed since vanish (PR #6677 did exactly this, 135 insertions / 136 deletions of pure collateral). Any other database-derived path likewise. The human-authored config â€” `.beads/README.md`, `.beads/config.yaml`, `.beads/.gitignore`, `.beads/hooks/**` â€” IS fair game. CLAUDE.md's Beads durability section is the authority.
6. Beads touching tools/xray/ update tools/xray/spec/* in the same PR (or state "spec unchanged because X").
7. Hot-zone files only if this bead flags them â€” and the hot zone INCLUDES the spec/*.md hot files (spec/004-Views.md, spec/002-Frames.md, spec/API.md, spec/Conventions.md among others), not just implementation/shadow-cljs.edn, implementation/deps.edn and .github/workflows/*. CLAUDE.md's Workflow section carries the canonical list; read it there rather than treating this line as complete.
8. No AI attribution in commits or PRs.
9. If you created a node_modules junction, remove it as your last act.
10. Checkpoint findings become real bd issues AND a row in docs/design/hicasso/product/correction-ledger.md. The checkpoint's own report PR writes the `open` row; a CORRECTIVE PR never edits that file â€” every later transition is the ledger keeper's. Read the file's own stated protocol before touching it.

description:
Review the `reagent-fresco-migration` skill: skills/reagent-fresco-migration/, meaning SKILL.md and every reference and script under it. Do it in four SERIAL passes, finishing each one, and fixing what it finds, before starting the next:

Also look for references the SKILL.md points at that are missing or empty.
2. CORRECTNESS. Check every claim against spec/ and implementation/ at trunk: API names, signatures, keywords, reserved namespaces, file paths, commands and code examples. Look for names that no longer exist, behaviour that has changed, dead links, and examples that would not compile or run as written.
3. ORGANISATION AND STRUCTURE. SKILL.md should be a concise entry point. References should be split by topic, sit one level deep, and be linked directly from SKILL.md. Nothing should be duplicated across files, terminology should be consistent, and a reader should find what they need in the order they need it.
4. SKILL BEST PRACTICE (Anthropic's Agent Skills authoring guidance).
   - Frontmatter: `name`, and a `description` in the third person that says what the skill does AND when to use it, with specific trigger terms.
   - A lean SKILL.md body (well under ~500 lines) that uses progressive disclosure into reference files.
   - No time-sensitive or history narrative.
   - Concrete examples, and checklists for workflows where order matters.
   - Scripts for deterministic operations rather than prose instructions.

Report findings outside skills/reagent-fresco-migration/ (spec/, implementation/, skills/README.md, another skill) rather than editing them. skills/README.md is shared by every skill, so name any change it needs and do not make it.

POSTURE: fix real defects and improve structure where that pays a reader. Do not rewrite for style. Present-tense convention: no bead ids and no history in the skill text.

title: Test-suite pruning, fifth pass: tools/story-mcp
description:
Child of rf2-nvxtm (test-suite pruning, fifth pass). One worktree, one PR.

SURFACE: tools/story-mcp. This is the surface of rf2-txsk5.28 (fourth pass). Read rf2-txsk5.28 first: its description, notes and close reason. Together they give the runners and lanes, the count floors, the surface's cautions, the covers it relied on, and what the fourth pass already pruned. rf2-txsk5.28 gives the exact files in scope, or names the third-pass bead (rf2-n6gq4.28) that does. Confirm the scope and the runners yourself at tip in step 1, and report the delta.

<DIR> in the prompt below means this surface.

REPO MECHANICS: read rf2-nvxtm's description. Its count-floor, CLJS-lane, test-name, cross-surface-cover, hot-zone, plant and one-PR rules apply in full, and they win over anything in the prompt that seems to conflict.

== THE PROMPT (verbatim from Mike's local prompt file, which is not checked in; also in rf2-nvxtm's description)

Simplify the unit tests under tools/story-mcp. Do not change the code under test. LLMs tend to
write too many low-value unit tests, and this suite was largely written by them.

Assume the suite has more tests than it needs, and that many of its tests are longer
than they need to be. Every test costs CI time, reading time and refactoring friction,
and the low-value ones hide the tests that matter. I want a lean suite: each test earns
its place by guarding a behaviour a caller relies on, against a regression that could
plausibly happen and would matter. Each surviving test should be as short as the thing
it proves.

Stay inside tools/story-mcp. Do not edit tests elsewhere. If a deletion relies on a test outside
tools/story-mcp to keep covering something, name that test in your report.

Work in this order:
1. Run the suite and record the result: tests, assertions, failures, lines. Confirm a
   runner actually executes each file in tools/story-mcp; a file nothing runs cannot be pruned on
   evidence, so report it.
2. Read the code under test and list what it promises its callers: normal results, each
   boundary that takes its own path, each promised failure, and any past bug the tests
   refer to.
3. Map every test to the promise it checks. Most of the work shows up in this map:
   promises with five tests, tests with no promise, and tests of something no caller
   relies on.
4. Decide each test: keep, simplify, merge or delete.
5. Run the suite again and prove the pruned suite still guards every promise.

Work in small batches by contract group, and commit as you go. Before each batch,
predict the change in test and assertion counts; after it, confirm the counts moved by
exactly that much. If helper agents are available, use read-only ones for the mapping
step. If tools/story-mcp plainly will not finish in about four hours, stop at a group boundary,
ship what is done, and list the files you did not reach.

Decide each test with two questions:
- If this test were deleted, what bug could ship that no remaining test would catch?
  If you cannot name one, delete it.
- If you can name one: is that bug plausible in this code, would a caller notice it,
  and would nothing else surface it at once (a compile or load error, a boot-time
  validation, most of the suite going red)? If the bug is implausible, harmless, or
  loud anyway, delete the test.

Delete:
- A test another test implies. If A cannot pass while B fails, drop B.
- Extra examples of one behaviour that take the same path through the code.
- Existence and smoke checks: a function exists, a var resolves, something "is
  registered", a result is non-nil, a call "does not throw", when another test
  exercises the same call with a real assertion.
- Change detectors: a test that copies a constant, a data table, a default config, a
  roster or a string out of the source and asserts equality. It fails on every intended
  change and catches no bug. The exception is a value callers depend on exactly, such as
  a public id or a documented default, that nothing else pins: keep one test for it.
- Absence checks for things nothing produces, and negative-input tests for inputs no
  caller passes and the contract does not mention.
- Exhaustive enumeration: one row per enum member, keyword or field when they all take
  one path. Keep one representative plus the members that take a different path.
- Tests of the language, a library or the framework: a constructor sets a field, a
  getter returns it, a map holds the key just put in it.
- Tests that pin how the code works instead of what it does: private helpers already
  exercised through the public path, call order, internal data shapes, greps of the
  implementation's own source, and log, trace or error wording that is not part of the
  contract.
- Tests whose expected value is computed by the same logic as the code under test.
- Assertions that a mock returned what it was told to return, and tests whose mock setup
  is most of the test while the assertion checks the mock.
- Separate per-platform test files asserting the same thing about platform-neutral code.
  A single shared test that runs on both platforms is one test, not two: keep it.
- Tests of test helpers and fixtures.
- Tests of code that has no logic in it, and tests whose only subject is production code
  that no production caller uses.

Simplify every test you keep:
- Assert the whole result with one equality instead of one assertion per field. Drop an
  assertion that a later one in the same test implies.
- Cut setup, fixtures and data to what the assertion needs. Remove unused bindings,
  requires, helpers and fixtures.
- Tests that vary one input become one table-driven test. Keep the boundary rows and
  drop the mid-range ones.
- Tests that repeat the same setup for one assertion each become one test.
- Delete comments and docstrings that restate the code or narrate history. Keep a
  one-line why where a test's purpose is not obvious from its name and body.
- Rename a test only when its name no longer says what it asserts, and first check that
  nothing matches on the name, such as a CI filter, a skip list or a doc that cites it.

Keep, however small:
- The only test of a promise a caller relies on: a normal result, a boundary that takes
  a different path (empty, one, many; zero; the limit and one past it), a promised
  failure.
- A regression test for a bug that actually happened, unless a stronger test now covers
  it.
- The last guard of a security, privacy or redaction promise.
- The last test that keeps a gate able to fail, and the last test holding a published
  doc or spec claim to the code.
When a weak test and a strong test overlap, keep the strong one: the one that would fail
on more bugs.

Do not:
- Weaken an assertion, or swap an exact check for a looser one, to make a merge or a
  simplification easier.
- Delete a test because it fails, is slow or is flaky. Report it.
- Leave unused helpers, fixtures or requires behind.
- Add new tests. If you find a promise with no test, report it.
- Change production code. Dead code and stale docs or spec text go in your report as a
  list, not into your change.
If anything pins test counts or names, such as a count floor or a roster, update it in
the same change. Commit one file or module at a time.

Prove it:
- The suite passes before and after. Report both sets of counts.
- For each group of deletions that rests on a surviving cover, break the code in a place
  the deleted tests guarded and confirm a surviving test fails. Then restore the code and
  confirm it matches the committed file. One plant per group sharing a cover is enough.
  If nothing fails, you removed real coverage: put the tests back.
- A cover must actually run. A skipped test, a fixture the runner never loads, or a test
  on a lane nothing executes covers nothing. Confirm the runner executes a cover before
  resting a deletion on it.
- Run each test file you touched on its own at least once. Deleting a file can break a
  sibling that relied on it loading something first; give such a file its own require.
- A deletion made under the second question needs no plant. Give its one-line reason in
  the report instead.
- A simplification must not change what a test can catch. Where you removed an
  assertion, name the assertion that implies it.

Report:
- Before and after: tests, assertions, lines.
- Deleted tests, grouped by reason. For each, the surviving cover, or the one-line
  reason it was not worth keeping.
- Merges and simplifications: what went into what, and the lines each file lost.
- Notable keeps: tests you considered deleting but kept, and why.
- Plants, and which test caught each.
- Tests outside tools/story-mcp that your deletions rely on.
- Dead code, stale docs or spec text, and gaps (promises with no test). One line each.

If you are unsure whether a promise a caller relies on is still covered, keep the test
and say so. Losing the only guard of a real promise is still the one mistake that matters
more than leaving an extra test in. But being unsure whether a test is worth keeping is
not a reason to keep it. If you cannot say in one line what plausible regression it
catches that a caller would notice, delete it.

title: http stubs: no test runs with-request-stubs in a frame made with :images since make-frame {} went live
description:
FENCE: do not dispatch until PR #11247 (rf2-ji6cc) MERGES. It edits the same two test files. Clears when #11247 merges.

http stubs lost their image-loaded-frame coverage when the default frame went live. The stub target for with-request-stubs is registered when its namespace loads, so that a frame whose image generation was sealed before the stubs were installed still resolves it. Two tests covered that case: stubs-intercept-inside-pre-created-sealed-frame-rf2-bxc8kf in implementation/http/test/re_frame/http_managed_test.clj, and its -cljs- twin in implementation/adapters/reagent/test/re_frame/http_managed_cljs_test.cljs. Both build their frame with (make-frame {}). Since rf2-bmrh9 (#11235), that frame seals no generation and resolves the live store, so neither test exercises a sealed frame any more. No http test runs with-request-stubs inside a frame made with :images. The rf2-ji6cc worker found this (PR #11247).

Fix: add one variant of each test that builds its frame with :images, which seals a generation, before installing the stubs, and asserts the stub still intercepts. While there, drop "sealed" from the two existing test names, since they no longer build a sealed frame. Smallest change; reproduce the coverage by planting a fault, e.g. registering the stub target late, so that the new test goes red.

title: durable-target silently drops a mapped continuation, and the reply data-only walker misses lists, map keys and unknown host objects
description:
`durable-target` silently drops a mapped continuation, and the reply data-only walker misses lists, map keys and unknown host objects. Both holes sit at the durable boundary that resources uses: `resources/events.cljc` and `mutation_events.cljc` call `(rf.reply/durable-target reply-to)` before storing into the work ledger.

## 1. Silent loss of a mapping

In `implementation/core/src/re_frame/reply.cljc`, `durable-target` (~L435) does `(apply dissoc d ephemeral-target-keys)` (~L448). That strips the `::post` which `complete` applies (`(if post (post base) base)`). A target mapped with `(fn [e] [:parent/relay e])` therefore completes differently once it has been stored, yet the docstring promises it "fails LOUD".

`map-completed-event` stays: rf2-vfp6f kept it, citing Managed-Effects' SHOULD. So:
- Throw `:rf.error/reply-non-data-target` from `durable-target` when `::post` is present.
- Optional: make `(map-completed-event identity t)` return a target without `::post`, so that identity-mapped targets stay durable.

## 2. A deny-list walker

`walk-find-host-handle` recurses only into map values, vectors and sets, and returns nil for anything else. So all of these pass:
- `[:e (list f)]`;
- a function used as a map key;
- an atom;
- an unlisted JS or Java object.

`re-frame.recordable/explain-non-recordable` is already an allow-list that walks keys and every sequential. Route `validate-reply` and `durable-target` through it, with a leaf-policy option that refuses instants (replies use epoch-ms longs).

Leave the bounded payload-lint walker (`walk-find-host-handle-bounded` / `payload-host-handle?`) as it is. Add no new error ids.

## Gates and provenance

No hot-zone file; `spec/Managed-Effects.md` is not hot. Gates: core JVM, plus `npm run test:cljs` for the CLJS host (that needs a lane grant).

Supporting detail, local to this machine only: `C:\Users\miket\code\re-frame2\ai\findings\advisarial-review\sol-history\2026-10-15-low-hanging-fruit\before\06-core-replies-timers.md` §2-3, and `C:\Users\miket\code\re-frame2\ai\findings\advisarial-review\opus-history\2026-10-15-low-hanging-fruit\before\core-event-pipeline.md` D10.

title: Unit-test pruning: schemas
description:
Apply Mike's pruning prompt to implementation/schemas/test recursively in an isolated worker worktree. This is a distinct cluster in rf2-0wcq5. Push a test-only draft PR, babysit all checks until green, then mark ready; do not merge. Report no-op with evidence instead of manufacturing changes.

Simplify the unit tests under implementation/schemas/test. Do not change the code under test. LLMs tend to
write too many low-value unit tests, and this suite was largely written by them.

Assume the suite has more tests than it needs, and that many of its tests are longer
than they need to be. Every test costs CI time, reading time and refactoring friction,
and the low-value ones hide the tests that matter. I want a lean suite: each test earns
its place by guarding a behaviour a caller relies on, against a regression that could
plausibly happen and would matter. Each surviving test should be as short as the thing
it proves.

Stay inside implementation/schemas/test. Do not edit tests elsewhere. If a deletion relies on a test outside
implementation/schemas/test to keep covering something, name that test in your report.

Work in this order:
1. Run the suite and record the result: tests, assertions, failures, lines. Confirm a
   runner actually executes each file in implementation/schemas/test; a file nothing runs cannot be pruned on
   evidence, so report it.
2. Read the code under test and list what it promises its callers: normal results, each
   boundary that takes its own path, each promised failure, and any past bug the tests
   refer to.
3. Map every test to the promise it checks. Most of the work shows up in this map:
   promises with five tests, tests with no promise, and tests of something no caller
   relies on.
4. Decide each test: keep, simplify, merge or delete.
5. Run the suite again and prove the pruned suite still guards every promise.

Work in small batches by contract group, and commit as you go. Before each batch,
predict the change in test and assertion counts; after it, confirm the counts moved by
exactly that much. If helper agents are available, use read-only ones for the mapping
step. If implementation/schemas/test plainly will not finish in about four hours, stop at a group boundary,
ship what is done, and list the files you did not reach.

Decide each test with two questions:
- If this test were deleted, what bug could ship that no remaining test would catch?
  If you cannot name one, delete it.
- If you can name one: is that bug plausible in this code, would a caller notice it,
  and would nothing else surface it at once (a compile or load error, a boot-time
  validation, most of the suite going red)? If the bug is implausible, harmless, or
  loud anyway, delete the test.

Delete:
- A test another test implies. If A cannot pass while B fails, drop B.
- Extra examples of one behaviour that take the same path through the code.
- Existence and smoke checks: a function exists, a var resolves, something "is
  registered", a result is non-nil, a call "does not throw", when another test
  exercises the same call with a real assertion.
- Change detectors: a test that copies a constant, a data table, a default config, a
  roster or a string out of the source and asserts equality. It fails on every intended
  change and catches no bug. The exception is a value callers depend on exactly, such as
  a public id or a documented default, that nothing else pins: keep one test for it.
- Absence checks for things nothing produces, and negative-input tests for inputs no
  caller passes and the contract does not mention.
- Exhaustive enumeration: one row per enum member, keyword or field when they all take
  one path. Keep one representative plus the members that take a different path.
- Tests of the language, a library or the framework: a constructor sets a field, a
  getter returns it, a map holds the key just put in it.
- Tests that pin how the code works instead of what it does: private helpers already
  exercised through the public path, call order, internal data shapes, greps of the
  implementation's own source, and log, trace or error wording that is not part of the
  contract.
- Tests whose expected value is computed by the same logic as the code under test.
- Assertions that a mock returned what it was told to return, and tests whose mock setup
  is most of the test while the assertion checks the mock.
- Separate per-platform test files asserting the same thing about platform-neutral code.
  A single shared test that runs on both platforms is one test, not two: keep it.
- Tests of test helpers and fixtures.
- Tests of code that has no logic in it, and tests whose only subject is production code
  that no production caller uses.

Simplify every test you keep:
- Assert the whole result with one equality instead of one assertion per field. Drop an
  assertion that a later one in the same test implies.
- Cut setup, fixtures and data to what the assertion needs. Remove unused bindings,
  requires, helpers and fixtures.
- Tests that vary one input become one table-driven test. Keep the boundary rows and
  drop the mid-range ones.
- Tests that repeat the same setup for one assertion each become one test.
- Delete comments and docstrings that restate the code or narrate history. Keep a
  one-line why where a test's purpose is not obvious from its name and body.
- Rename a test only when its name no longer says what it asserts, and first check that
  nothing matches on the name, such as a CI filter, a skip list or a doc that cites it.

Keep, however small:
- The only test of a promise a caller relies on: a normal result, a boundary that takes
  a different path (empty, one, many; zero; the limit and one past it), a promised
  failure.
- A regression test for a bug that actually happened, unless a stronger test now covers
  it.
- The last guard of a security, privacy or redaction promise.
- The last test that keeps a gate able to fail, and the last test holding a published
  doc or spec claim to the code.
When a weak test and a strong test overlap, keep the strong one: the one that would fail
on more bugs.

Do not:
- Weaken an assertion, or swap an exact check for a looser one, to make a merge or a
  simplification easier.
- Delete a test because it fails, is slow or is flaky. Report it.
- Leave unused helpers, fixtures or requires behind.
- Add new tests. If you find a promise with no test, report it.
- Change production code. Dead code and stale docs or spec text go in your report as a
  list, not into your change.
If anything pins test counts or names, such as a count floor or a roster, update it in
the same change. Commit one file or module at a time.

Prove it:
- The suite passes before and after. Report both sets of counts.
- For each group of deletions that rests on a surviving cover, break the code in a place
  the deleted tests guarded and confirm a surviving test fails. Then restore the code and
  confirm it matches the committed file. One plant per group sharing a cover is enough.
  If nothing fails, you removed real coverage: put the tests back.
- A cover must actually run. A skipped test, a fixture the runner never loads, or a test
  on a lane nothing executes covers nothing. Confirm the runner executes a cover before
  resting a deletion on it.
- Run each test file you touched on its own at least once. Deleting a file can break a
  sibling that relied on it loading something first; give such a file its own require.
- A deletion made under the second question needs no plant. Give its one-line reason in
  the report instead.
- A simplification must not change what a test can catch. Where you removed an
  assertion, name the assertion that implies it.

Report:
- Before and after: tests, assertions, lines.
- Deleted tests, grouped by reason. For each, the surviving cover, or the one-line
  reason it was not worth keeping.
- Merges and simplifications: what went into what, and the lines each file lost.
- Notable keeps: tests you considered deleting but kept, and why.
- Plants, and which test caught each.
- Tests outside implementation/schemas/test that your deletions rely on.
- Dead code, stale docs or spec text, and gaps (promises with no test). One line each.

If you are unsure whether a promise a caller relies on is still covered, keep the test
and say so. Losing the only guard of a real promise is still the one mistake that matters
more than leaving an extra test in. But being unsure whether a test is worth keeping is
not a reason to keep it. If you cannot say in one line what plausible regression it
catches that a caller would notice, delete it.

description:
Optional-artefact coordinates are restated in ten places, and one copy has already drifted. Derive them from `feature-registry`, so each coordinate is written once.

title: Unit-test pruning: test-quiet
description:
Apply the exact requested pruning prompt recursively to implementation/test-quiet/test. This is a distinct worker cluster under rf2-0wcq5. Production code remains unchanged except temporary hash-verified fault plants. Push a draft test-only PR, babysit all latest-head checks to green, then mark ready. A measured no-op or unexecuted-file report is valid; do not manufacture changes.

Simplify the unit tests under implementation/test-quiet/test. Do not change the code under test. LLMs tend to
write too many low-value unit tests, and this suite was largely written by them.

Assume the suite has more tests than it needs, and that many of its tests are longer
than they need to be. Every test costs CI time, reading time and refactoring friction,
and the low-value ones hide the tests that matter. I want a lean suite: each test earns
its place by guarding a behaviour a caller relies on, against a regression that could
plausibly happen and would matter. Each surviving test should be as short as the thing
it proves.

Stay inside implementation/test-quiet/test. Do not edit tests elsewhere. If a deletion relies on a test outside
implementation/test-quiet/test to keep covering something, name that test in your report.

Work in this order:
1. Run the suite and record the result: tests, assertions, failures, lines. Confirm a
   runner actually executes each file in implementation/test-quiet/test; a file nothing runs cannot be pruned on
   evidence, so report it.
2. Read the code under test and list what it promises its callers: normal results, each
   boundary that takes its own path, each promised failure, and any past bug the tests
   refer to.
3. Map every test to the promise it checks. Most of the work shows up in this map:
   promises with five tests, tests with no promise, and tests of something no caller
   relies on.
4. Decide each test: keep, simplify, merge or delete.
5. Run the suite again and prove the pruned suite still guards every promise.

Work in small batches by contract group, and commit as you go. Before each batch,
predict the change in test and assertion counts; after it, confirm the counts moved by
exactly that much. If helper agents are available, use read-only ones for the mapping
step. If implementation/test-quiet/test plainly will not finish in about four hours, stop at a group boundary,
ship what is done, and list the files you did not reach.

Decide each test with two questions:
- If this test were deleted, what bug could ship that no remaining test would catch?
  If you cannot name one, delete it.
- If you can name one: is that bug plausible in this code, would a caller notice it,
  and would nothing else surface it at once (a compile or load error, a boot-time
  validation, most of the suite going red)? If the bug is implausible, harmless, or
  loud anyway, delete the test.

Delete:
- A test another test implies. If A cannot pass while B fails, drop B.
- Extra examples of one behaviour that take the same path through the code.
- Existence and smoke checks: a function exists, a var resolves, something "is
  registered", a result is non-nil, a call "does not throw", when another test
  exercises the same call with a real assertion.
- Change detectors: a test that copies a constant, a data table, a default config, a
  roster or a string out of the source and asserts equality. It fails on every intended
  change and catches no bug. The exception is a value callers depend on exactly, such as
  a public id or a documented default, that nothing else pins: keep one test for it.
- Absence checks for things nothing produces, and negative-input tests for inputs no
  caller passes and the contract does not mention.
- Exhaustive enumeration: one row per enum member, keyword or field when they all take
  one path. Keep one representative plus the members that take a different path.
- Tests of the language, a library or the framework: a constructor sets a field, a
  getter returns it, a map holds the key just put in it.
- Tests that pin how the code works instead of what it does: private helpers already
  exercised through the public path, call order, internal data shapes, greps of the
  implementation's own source, and log, trace or error wording that is not part of the
  contract.
- Tests whose expected value is computed by the same logic as the code under test.
- Assertions that a mock returned what it was told to return, and tests whose mock setup
  is most of the test while the assertion checks the mock.
- Separate per-platform test files asserting the same thing about platform-neutral code.
  A single shared test that runs on both platforms is one test, not two: keep it.
- Tests of test helpers and fixtures.
- Tests of code that has no logic in it, and tests whose only subject is production code
  that no production caller uses.

Simplify every test you keep:
- Assert the whole result with one equality instead of one assertion per field. Drop an
  assertion that a later one in the same test implies.
- Cut setup, fixtures and data to what the assertion needs. Remove unused bindings,
  requires, helpers and fixtures.
- Tests that vary one input become one table-driven test. Keep the boundary rows and
  drop the mid-range ones.
- Tests that repeat the same setup for one assertion each become one test.
- Delete comments and docstrings that restate the code or narrate history. Keep a
  one-line why where a test's purpose is not obvious from its name and body.
- Rename a test only when its name no longer says what it asserts, and first check that
  nothing matches on the name, such as a CI filter, a skip list or a doc that cites it.

Keep, however small:
- The only test of a promise a caller relies on: a normal result, a boundary that takes
  a different path (empty, one, many; zero; the limit and one past it), a promised
  failure.
- A regression test for a bug that actually happened, unless a stronger test now covers
  it.
- The last guard of a security, privacy or redaction promise.
- The last test that keeps a gate able to fail, and the last test holding a published
  doc or spec claim to the code.
When a weak test and a strong test overlap, keep the strong one: the one that would fail
on more bugs.

Do not:
- Weaken an assertion, or swap an exact check for a looser one, to make a merge or a
  simplification easier.
- Delete a test because it fails, is slow or is flaky. Report it.
- Leave unused helpers, fixtures or requires behind.
- Add new tests. If you find a promise with no test, report it.
- Change production code. Dead code and stale docs or spec text go in your report as a
  list, not into your change.
If anything pins test counts or names, such as a count floor or a roster, update it in
the same change. Commit one file or module at a time.

Prove it:
- The suite passes before and after. Report both sets of counts.
- For each group of deletions that rests on a surviving cover, break the code in a place
  the deleted tests guarded and confirm a surviving test fails. Then restore the code and
  confirm it matches the committed file. One plant per group sharing a cover is enough.
  If nothing fails, you removed real coverage: put the tests back.
- A cover must actually run. A skipped test, a fixture the runner never loads, or a test
  on a lane nothing executes covers nothing. Confirm the runner executes a cover before
  resting a deletion on it.
- Run each test file you touched on its own at least once. Deleting a file can break a
  sibling that relied on it loading something first; give such a file its own require.
- A deletion made under the second question needs no plant. Give its one-line reason in
  the report instead.
- A simplification must not change what a test can catch. Where you removed an
  assertion, name the assertion that implies it.

Report:
- Before and after: tests, assertions, lines.
- Deleted tests, grouped by reason. For each, the surviving cover, or the one-line
  reason it was not worth keeping.
- Merges and simplifications: what went into what, and the lines each file lost.
- Notable keeps: tests you considered deleting but kept, and why.
- Plants, and which test caught each.
- Tests outside implementation/test-quiet/test that your deletions rely on.
- Dead code, stale docs or spec text, and gaps (promises with no test). One line each.

If you are unsure whether a promise a caller relies on is still covered, keep the test
and say so. Losing the only guard of a real promise is still the one mistake that matters
more than leaving an extra test in. But being unsure whether a test is worth keeping is
not a reason to keep it. If you cannot say in one line what plausible regression it
catches that a caller would notice, delete it.
notes:
Dispatch coordination: /root serializes all bd access. The worker completes bounded recursive review, baseline/final counts, coverage controls, final rebase/push and source handoff. After accepting the exact final source head and self-contained note, /root owns all final-head CI watching/fixes, marks ready only after all checks/workflows are terminal green, and closes the issue. Source handoff with a draft PR is not completion.

title: Unit-test pruning: reagent-slim
description:
Apply the exact requested pruning prompt recursively to implementation/adapters/reagent-slim/test. This is a distinct worker cluster under rf2-0wcq5. Production code remains unchanged except temporary hash-verified fault plants. Push a draft test-only PR, babysit all latest-head checks to green, then mark ready. A measured no-op or unexecuted-file report is valid; do not manufacture changes.

Simplify the unit tests under implementation/adapters/reagent-slim/test. Do not change the code under test. LLMs tend to
write too many low-value unit tests, and this suite was largely written by them.

Assume the suite has more tests than it needs, and that many of its tests are longer
than they need to be. Every test costs CI time, reading time and refactoring friction,
and the low-value ones hide the tests that matter. I want a lean suite: each test earns
its place by guarding a behaviour a caller relies on, against a regression that could
plausibly happen and would matter. Each surviving test should be as short as the thing
it proves.

Stay inside implementation/adapters/reagent-slim/test. Do not edit tests elsewhere. If a deletion relies on a test outside
implementation/adapters/reagent-slim/test to keep covering something, name that test in your report.

Work in this order:
1. Run the suite and record the result: tests, assertions, failures, lines. Confirm a
   runner actually executes each file in implementation/adapters/reagent-slim/test; a file nothing runs cannot be pruned on
   evidence, so report it.
2. Read the code under test and list what it promises its callers: normal results, each
   boundary that takes its own path, each promised failure, and any past bug the tests
   refer to.
3. Map every test to the promise it checks. Most of the work shows up in this map:
   promises with five tests, tests with no promise, and tests of something no caller
   relies on.
4. Decide each test: keep, simplify, merge or delete.
5. Run the suite again and prove the pruned suite still guards every promise.

Work in small batches by contract group, and commit as you go. Before each batch,
predict the change in test and assertion counts; after it, confirm the counts moved by
exactly that much. If helper agents are available, use read-only ones for the mapping
step. If implementation/adapters/reagent-slim/test plainly will not finish in about four hours, stop at a group boundary,
ship what is done, and list the files you did not reach.

Decide each test with two questions:
- If this test were deleted, what bug could ship that no remaining test would catch?
  If you cannot name one, delete it.
- If you can name one: is that bug plausible in this code, would a caller notice it,
  and would nothing else surface it at once (a compile or load error, a boot-time
  validation, most of the suite going red)? If the bug is implausible, harmless, or
  loud anyway, delete the test.

Delete:
- A test another test implies. If A cannot pass while B fails, drop B.
- Extra examples of one behaviour that take the same path through the code.
- Existence and smoke checks: a function exists, a var resolves, something "is
  registered", a result is non-nil, a call "does not throw", when another test
  exercises the same call with a real assertion.
- Change detectors: a test that copies a constant, a data table, a default config, a
  roster or a string out of the source and asserts equality. It fails on every intended
  change and catches no bug. The exception is a value callers depend on exactly, such as
  a public id or a documented default, that nothing else pins: keep one test for it.
- Absence checks for things nothing produces, and negative-input tests for inputs no
  caller passes and the contract does not mention.
- Exhaustive enumeration: one row per enum member, keyword or field when they all take
  one path. Keep one representative plus the members that take a different path.
- Tests of the language, a library or the framework: a constructor sets a field, a
  getter returns it, a map holds the key just put in it.
- Tests that pin how the code works instead of what it does: private helpers already
  exercised through the public path, call order, internal data shapes, greps of the
  implementation's own source, and log, trace or error wording that is not part of the
  contract.
- Tests whose expected value is computed by the same logic as the code under test.
- Assertions that a mock returned what it was told to return, and tests whose mock setup
  is most of the test while the assertion checks the mock.
- Separate per-platform test files asserting the same thing about platform-neutral code.
  A single shared test that runs on both platforms is one test, not two: keep it.
- Tests of test helpers and fixtures.
- Tests of code that has no logic in it, and tests whose only subject is production code
  that no production caller uses.

Simplify every test you keep:
- Assert the whole result with one equality instead of one assertion per field. Drop an
  assertion that a later one in the same test implies.
- Cut setup, fixtures and data to what the assertion needs. Remove unused bindings,
  requires, helpers and fixtures.
- Tests that vary one input become one table-driven test. Keep the boundary rows and
  drop the mid-range ones.
- Tests that repeat the same setup for one assertion each become one test.
- Delete comments and docstrings that restate the code or narrate history. Keep a
  one-line why where a test's purpose is not obvious from its name and body.
- Rename a test only when its name no longer says what it asserts, and first check that
  nothing matches on the name, such as a CI filter, a skip list or a doc that cites it.

Keep, however small:
- The only test of a promise a caller relies on: a normal result, a boundary that takes
  a different path (empty, one, many; zero; the limit and one past it), a promised
  failure.
- A regression test for a bug that actually happened, unless a stronger test now covers
  it.
- The last guard of a security, privacy or redaction promise.
- The last test that keeps a gate able to fail, and the last test holding a published
  doc or spec claim to the code.
When a weak test and a strong test overlap, keep the strong one: the one that would fail
on more bugs.

Do not:
- Weaken an assertion, or swap an exact check for a looser one, to make a merge or a
  simplification easier.
- Delete a test because it fails, is slow or is flaky. Report it.
- Leave unused helpers, fixtures or requires behind.
- Add new tests. If you find a promise with no test, report it.
- Change production code. Dead code and stale docs or spec text go in your report as a
  list, not into your change.
If anything pins test counts or names, such as a count floor or a roster, update it in
the same change. Commit one file or module at a time.

Prove it:
- The suite passes before and after. Report both sets of counts.
- For each group of deletions that rests on a surviving cover, break the code in a place
  the deleted tests guarded and confirm a surviving test fails. Then restore the code and
  confirm it matches the committed file. One plant per group sharing a cover is enough.
  If nothing fails, you removed real coverage: put the tests back.
- A cover must actually run. A skipped test, a fixture the runner never loads, or a test
  on a lane nothing executes covers nothing. Confirm the runner executes a cover before
  resting a deletion on it.
- Run each test file you touched on its own at least once. Deleting a file can break a
  sibling that relied on it loading something first; give such a file its own require.
- A deletion made under the second question needs no plant. Give its one-line reason in
  the report instead.
- A simplification must not change what a test can catch. Where you removed an
  assertion, name the assertion that implies it.

Report:
- Before and after: tests, assertions, lines.
- Deleted tests, grouped by reason. For each, the surviving cover, or the one-line
  reason it was not worth keeping.
- Merges and simplifications: what went into what, and the lines each file lost.
- Notable keeps: tests you considered deleting but kept, and why.
- Plants, and which test caught each.
- Tests outside implementation/adapters/reagent-slim/test that your deletions rely on.
- Dead code, stale docs or spec text, and gaps (promises with no test). One line each.

If you are unsure whether a promise a caller relies on is still covered, keep the test
and say so. Losing the only guard of a real promise is still the one mistake that matters
more than leaving an extra test in. But being unsure whether a test is worth keeping is
not a reason to keep it. If you cannot say in one line what plausible regression it
catches that a caller would notice, delete it.

title: Route every navigation door through one internal navigate* pipeline, and give raw {:url} requests not-found semantics on a schema miss
description:
## Ruling

Routing's navigation doors run through ONE internal pipeline function, `navigate*`, instead of two hand-written orchestrations. Today `navigate-handler` (for `:rf.route/navigate`) and `url-change-fx` (for `:rf.route/url-requested` and `:rf.route/handle-url-change`) each spell out the stage order of Spec 012 §The one planning pipeline themselves, calling shared helpers. After this bead, `navigate*` runs stages 1-7 once (validate, resolve, classify, leave, enter, plan, commit), and each of the three public events becomes a thin wrapper that supplies its inputs as data: the source (a named address, a raw URL, or an in-place edit), the cause, `url-driven?` (push/replace after commit, or no push plus restore-by-replace on block/deny), the default scroll, and continue's one-shot leave bypass. Stage 2 is the only fork, and it forks on SOURCE KIND, never on which event arrived.

One deliberate behaviour change: a raw URL gets user-input semantics whichever event carries it. `[:rf.route/navigate {:url u}]` where `u` matches a route but fails its `:params`/`:query` schema renders `:rf.route/not-found` with `:reason :validation`, exactly as `handle-url-change` does on the same `u`; and a `{:url}` route miss emits the same always-on route-miss record as the URL-driven door. A named address (`{:to ...}`) keeps its caller-error behaviour: a schema failure still emits `:rf.error/schema-validation-failure` and rejects.

All three public events stay. Whether to then delete `:rf.route/url-requested` is NOT part of this ruling (see Rejected options).

Decided 2026-10-16: Mike directed that every dossier recommendation an independent Codex review agreed with be actioned. Mike's instruction, verbatim:

> review all decisions. They now have a "Codex Recomendation" section.  Where the original
> recomendation matches the Code Recomendation, create a bead to action the decision.  And then
> remove the file.  Leave behind cases where the two differ materially.

Decisive facts, read in source at trunk 89517e8f54 (paths under `implementation/routing/src/re_frame/routing/`):

1. **The stage order is written twice.** `navigate-handler` is `navigate.cljc:185-649`; `url-change-fx` is `url_change.cljc:158-467`. Both call the same helpers (`address/classify`, `resolve/url-resolution`, `resolve/resolved-target`, `plan/fragment-only?`, `plan/scroll-plan`, `decisions/decide`, `resolve/route-plan`) but each sequences them itself. The fragment-only branch exists twice: `fragment-only-nav-fx` at `navigate.cljc:108-183` and `fragment-only-fx` at `url_change.cljc:109-156`. Only stages 6-7 are already one implementation: `commit-navigation` at `events.cljc:181-357`.
2. **One URL string, two meanings.** On a schema miss, `navigate {:url}` deliberately keeps the matched route id (comment at `navigate.cljc:280-292`) and rejects when `route-url` throws (`navigate.cljc:460-482`), while the same string through `url-requested` or `handle-url-change` becomes not-found via `url-resolution` (`resolve.cljc:217-249`, `validation-fail?` makes it a fallback). Spec 012 spends a paragraph and a table on the asymmetry (`spec/012-Routing.md:510`, `:817-827`). Route-miss telemetry also differs by door: the URL-driven miss adds `:rf.error/no-such-handler` (`url_change.cljc:383-418`, with a comment at `:409-412` calling it URL-driven-specific); the `navigate {:url}` miss emits only the shared fallback telemetry (`navigate.cljc:598-608`).
3. **The two copies are already drifting.** The `navigate.cljc:150-152` docstring says the programmatic fragment branch "must NOT copy `url_change.cljc`'s `fragment-only-fx` verbatim — that helper carries scroll CAPTURE only". That is false now: `fragment-only-fx` takes capture, push and scroll (`url_change.cljc:109-156`). And `route-transition-inputs` (`tooling.cljc:105-107`) names only `:rf.route/navigate` and `:rf.route/handle-url-change` as the route fact's writers, omitting `:rf.route/url-requested`, which commits the slice in its own event (`url-requested-handler` docstring, `url_change.cljc:586-600`).

Rejected options:

- **A, leave it and patch the small truths in place:** the drift pattern continues; every stage 1-5 feature (parent-chain `:can-enter`, `:query-merge` changes, any new policy key) has to be written into two orchestrations. It survives only as the fallback in the stop condition under Work.
- **C, also delete `:rf.route/url-requested` in the same move:** NOT ruled. The two reviews agree the event is redundant but disagree on what a `route-link` click should dispatch afterwards (its `{:to ...}` address, which bypasses route ranking, versus the generated path URL, which is rematched), so that step is held for Mike. This bead keeps `url-requested` and its link payload exactly as they are.

Supersedes: no standing ruling or EP. The result stays inside Spec 012's explicit allowance (`spec/012-Routing.md:903`: doors "may remain separate public events ... but they call the same resolver, decisions, planner, and commit assembler") and EP-0037 §One planning pipeline for every door (`docs/EP/EP-0037-route-planning-and-activation-ownership.md:397-400`), tightening "the same helpers" to "one function". It removes the per-door `{:url}` asymmetry that `012:510` and the `012:817-827` table document.

## Work

**Code** (`implementation/routing/src/re_frame/routing/`):

- Write `navigate*`: stages 1-7 once, ending in the unchanged `events/commit-navigation`. Input is roughly `{:source <address | {:url u} | in-place edit> :cause c :url-driven? bool}` plus policy. Where it lives (one of the two files, or a new pipeline namespace replacing both) is the implementer's call; the dossier estimated the two files (1,284 lines together) land at 700-850 lines, with roughly 100-150 lines of executable saving.
- `navigate-handler`, `url-requested-handler` (`url_change.cljc:586`) and the `:rf.route/handle-url-change` handler become wrappers of a few lines each. Per-door differences are wrapper inputs, never branches inside `navigate*`: links and programmatic requests commit state before push/replace; the already-moved URL doors (popstate, initial, SSR, host-pushed) emit no forward push and restore a blocked or denied URL by replace where reconstructible; SSR keeps its default 403 on denial; default scroll is `:top`, or `:restore` for `:popstate`/`:initial`/`:ssr`; cause selection (`url_change.cljc:469-518`) is unchanged.
- One fragment-only branch replaces both copies. The stale "must NOT copy" docstring at `navigate.cljc:150-152` goes with the duplicate.
- Stage 2 by source kind: an address resolves through `resolved-target` + `route-url` (caller-error behaviour unchanged); a raw URL goes through the external check, app-URL reduction and `match-url`, so a schema miss becomes not-found with `:reason :validation` and a miss emits the route-miss record plus `:rf.error/no-such-handler`; an in-place edit patches the current slice. Delete the comments that justify the old asymmetry (`navigate.cljc:280-292`, `url_change.cljc:409-412`).
- `tooling.cljc:105-107`: add `[:event :rf.route/url-requested]` to `route-transition-inputs`, and fix its docstring at `tooling.cljc:226-232`. Update the pin in `implementation/routing/test/re_frame/route_algebra_view_test.clj:55-56` and the worked example in `spec/Derivations.md:626-627` and `:784`. The same example also appears in `docs/EP/EP-0014-derivation-and-process-algebra.md:1054-1055`.
- No new async scheduler.

**Spec** (`spec/012-Routing.md`), five places:

- §Navigation is an event (`012:372`): the sketch shows the doors calling one function.
- §Target form (`012:510`): drop the "third case" schema-miss asymmetry; a raw URL renders not-found on a schema miss.
- §Validation-error surfacing across the three paths (`012:817-827`): a `{:url}` request joins the URL-driven not-found row; the `route-url` and `navigate {:to ...}` rows are unchanged.
- §The one planning pipeline (`012:887-903`): the doors call one function, and stage 2 forks on source kind.
- §Standard runtime events (`012:1183`): the rows for the three door events.

**Tests and fixtures:**

- New conformance fixture: a matched-but-schema-invalid `[:rf.route/navigate {:url ...}]` renders `:rf.route/not-found` with `:reason :validation`.
- Update any test asserting the old `{:url}` rejection or the missing `{:url}` route-miss record.
- Existing door law fixtures stay and must stay green unchanged: `spec/conformance/fixtures/routing-door-parity.edn`, `route-entry-denied.edn` (every door), `route-navigation-blocked.edn`.

**Deliberately stays:** all three public events and their ids; the link payload `[:rf.route/url-requested {:url path-url + policy}]` (`link.cljc:175-201`); the `:link` cause; `commit-navigation`; `:rf.route/prefetch` and `:rf.route/replan-resources` (they plan without navigating, so they are not doors); route readiness as it is (slice-cached, with the pruning latch accepted as EP-0037 OI-2); the nav-token kit (`:rf.route/nav-token` and `:rf.route/route-id` cofx, `:rf.route/with-nav-token`, `reply.cljc`).

**Stop condition.** If the merged pipeline does not shrink materially (`navigate*` ends up branching on door as often as the two copies do today), stop and land option A-plus instead: one shared fragment-only helper, one source-decided `{:url}` rule, and the `tooling.cljc` fix. Say so on this bead.

## Sequencing

- **Hot zones:** none. Edits `spec/012-Routing.md` and `spec/Derivations.md`, neither a hot zone.
- **Depends on:** nothing.
- **Followed by:** the `:on-match` target bead filed from the same ruling (it also edits `spec/012-Routing.md`; run sequentially, not in parallel).
- **Cross-dossier:** the held option C (delete `:rf.route/url-requested`) from dossier `routing-one-navigate-pipeline.md`, if Mike rules it, follows this bead. Dossier `ssr-server-init-reserved-name.md` concerns the SSR feed into `handle-url-change`; if its bead edits the SSR cause path in `url_change.cljc` or spec 012 §SSR, sequence the two.
- Does not touch `spec/011-SSR.md`.

## Evidence

Read in source at trunk 89517e8f54, and unchanged at 3aaacf1cde: the two orchestrations and fragment-only copies and their line ranges; the `{:url}` keep-the-matched-id comment and the `route-url` reject; the URL-driven fallback in `resolve.cljc`; the differing route-miss telemetry; the stale docstring; `route-transition-inputs` and its four mirrors; `url-requested-handler` committing in its own event; the `link.cljc` payload; the spec 012 lines cited.

Still needs a run: the actual size of the merged pipeline; that the routing JVM lane, `npm run test:cljs`, and the door-parity, entry-denied and navigation-blocked fixtures stay green; which existing tests pin the old `{:url}` behaviour.
acceptance_criteria:
1. One function runs stages 1-7 for every door. `navigate-handler`, `url-requested-handler` and the `:rf.route/handle-url-change` handler each only build its inputs (source, cause, url-driven?, default scroll, leave bypass) and call it; no door handler sequences stages 1-5 itself, and stage 2 branches on source kind, not on event id.
2. Exactly one fragment-only branch exists, and the "must NOT copy" docstring (`navigate.cljc:150-152` at trunk 89517e8f54) is gone.
3. `[:rf.route/navigate {:url u}]`, where `u` matches a route but fails its `:params` or `:query` schema, commits `:rf.route/not-found` with `:reason :validation`, identical to `:rf.route/handle-url-change` on the same `u`. A new conformance fixture pins this.
4. A `navigate {:url}` route miss emits the same always-on route-miss record and `:rf.error/no-such-handler` as the URL-driven door.
5. `[:rf.route/navigate {:to ...}]` with schema-invalid params still emits `:rf.error/schema-validation-failure` (`:where :event`), leaves the slice unchanged, and pushes nothing.
6. These laws hold unchanged: an exact no-op evaluates no guards and pushes nothing; a fragment-only move evaluates both guards, keeps the nav-token and skips activation work; a planning failure commits an addressable error target and dispatches none of its `:on-match` events; links and programmatic requests commit state before push/replace; popstate, initial, SSR and host-pushed doors push nothing and restore a blocked or denied URL by replace; SSR denial keeps its default 403; `:rf.route/continue` consumes the matching pending id and replays with one-shot leave bypass and entry rechecked; cancel clears only the matching pending question; trace causes are unchanged (`:link`, `:navigate`, `:popstate`, `:initial`, `:ssr`).
7. Link laws hold: guarded links, replace and scroll, non-owner frames and SSR hrefs keep their behaviour; a retained link closure from a destroyed frame still cannot navigate its same-id successor; modifier and native clicks keep anchor behaviour.
8. `route-transition-inputs` lists `:rf.route/navigate`, `:rf.route/url-requested` and `:rf.route/handle-url-change`, and `route_algebra_view_test.clj` and `spec/Derivations.md` agree with it.
9. Spec 012 is updated in its five places (§Navigation is an event, §Target form, §Validation-error surfacing across the three paths, §The one planning pipeline, §Standard runtime events), and no paragraph remains explaining a per-door difference in `{:url}` handling.
10. All three public door events, the `route-link` payload and the `:link` cause are unchanged.
11. Green, with the runner's own exit codes quoted in the PR: the routing JVM lane, `npm run test:cljs`, the door-parity, entry-denied and navigation-blocked fixtures, `mkdocs build --strict` and `scripts/check_doc_slugs.py`.
12. If the stop condition fired (the merged pipeline did not shrink materially), the bead records that and option A-plus landed instead: one fragment-only helper, one source-decided `{:url}` rule, and the `tooling.cljc` fix, meeting criteria 2-8 and 11.
notes:

Stage 2 is `resolve-address` (named address / in-place edit; `route-url` reject unchanged) or `resolve-raw-url`, chosen by `(contains? request :url)`. One `fragment-only-fx`; the "must NOT copy" docstring is gone with the duplicate. Size: navigate.cljc + url_change.cljc went from 1,284 lines to 657; non-comment code lines from 462 to 317.

Why url_change.cljc and not navigate.cljc or a new namespace: the always-on route-miss record (`dispatch-error-record!`) must stay in `re-frame.routing.url-change`, which `implementation/core/test/re_frame/egress_chokepoint_conformance_test.clj` allow-lists by namespace; the facade (`routing.cljc`, outside the fence) and the api-manifest generator name both namespaces, and the security test calls `rf.routing.navigate/navigate-handler`.
